1.title: 1. What a magician can do
1.content: Spellcasting . | Spells fall into five categories: Combat, Detection, Health, Illusion, Manipulation. (SR3 p.191–198) | You learn each spell at a specific Force. You can cast it at that Force or lower, never higher. (SR3 p.178) At character creation no spell can be bought above Force 6. (SR3 p.60) | Casting is a Complex Action: roll Sorcery plus up to as many Spell Pool dice as Sorcery dice. The TN is the target’s Willpower (mana spells) or Body (physical spells), or its Object Resistance. (SR3 p.107, p.182) | Drain: Power = Force ÷ 2 (round down) + the spell’s modifier, at the Damage Level shown. Resist with Willpower plus any number of Spell Pool dice, and reduce one level per 2 successes. (SR3 p.162, p.44) . | It’s Stun if the Force is no higher than your Magic, and Physical if it is higher, or if you’re astrally projecting. (SR3 p.162) | Every spell you’re sustaining adds +2 to Drain Power. (SR3 p.162) | . | Spell Pool = (INT + WIL + MAG) ÷ 3. (SR3 p.44) | . For the full step-by-step, including resistance, Spell Defense and Drain, see Spellcasting, Resistance & Drain. Conjuring . Hermetic mages call elementals: Earth, Air, Fire and Water. (SR3 p.186) . | You need a conjuring library and a hermetic circle, each rated at least the Force of the elemental, plus ritual materials costing about 1,000¥ × Force. (SR3 p.186; MitS p.169) | The elemental needs something to form from: a bonfire, a pool of water, and so on. (SR3 p.186) | An elemental can give five services: Aid Sorcery, Aid Study, Spell Sustaining, Physical Service, Remote Service. For Aid Sorcery, fire elementals help combat spells, air detection, water illusion and earth manipulation. No elemental helps health spells. (SR3 p.187) | . Shamans summon nature spirits, and only inside the spirit’s domain. (SR3 p.184, p.186) . | Summoning is an Exclusive Complex Action. The Conjuring Test is against TN = the spirit’s Force, and each success is one service. With no successes, nothing comes, but Drain still applies. (SR3 p.186) | Nature spirits vanish at sunrise and sunset, and any unused services are lost. (SR3 p.186) | A service is one use of one of the spirit’s powers, or a physical task such as attacking. (SR3 p.186) | The four families are (SR3 p.266–267): . | Spirits of Man: city, field, hearth | Spirits of the Land: desert, forest, mountain, prairie | Spirits of the Sky: mist, storm, wind | Spirits of the Waters: lake, river, sea, swamp | . | . Conjuring Drain: Power = the spirit’s Force, with the level set by comparing Force to your Charisma. Resist with Charisma. (SR3 p.162, p.187) . Ritual sorcery (MitS p.34–36) . | A team of magicians can cast one spell together. It builds over hours, but it can reach a target out of sight. | The team can have at most as many members as the lowest Sorcery rating among them. Everyone must know the spell at the chosen Force, and all must share a tradition (shamans of different totems may mix). | You need a hermetic circle or shamanic lodge rated at least the spell’s Force, plus ritual materials, which are used up whatever happens. | To reach a distant target you need a material link: a piece of the target, such as blood, hair or tissue. | Elemental manipulation spells can’t be cast as ritual sorcery. | . Foci (SR3 p.189–191; MitS p.169) . Foci are bonded with Karma. The core types are spell foci (one specific spell or a whole category), spirit foci, power foci, sustaining foci and weapon foci. Active foci are visible and vulnerable on the astral. A weapon focus lets you use an armed skill in astral combat.

2.title: 2. Astral space
2.content: Astral perception (SR3 p.171–172) . | It takes a Simple Action to switch. While perceiving you’re dual-natured: you see astral forms and auras, and they can attack you. | Assensing: Intelligence against TN 4, taking a Simple Action. With 1–2 successes you learn general health, whether cyberware is present, rough emotions, and mundane or Awakened. More successes give Essence and Magic compared to yours, implant locations and astral signatures. (SR3 p.172) | Doing ordinary, non-magical tasks while perceiving (shooting, driving) costs +2 TN. (SR3 p.172) | . Astral projection (SR3 p.172–173) . | Leaving your body and returning are each an Exclusive Complex Action. Your body lies in a trance. | Your body loses 1 Essence per hour you’re away. At 0 Essence you die. (SR3 p.173) | Normal movement is Intelligence × 4 m per turn. Fast movement is up to Magic in kilometers per turn, roughly Magic × 1,000 km per hour. (SR3 p.173) | Solid earth blocks astral forms, which is why secure sites are often built underground. (SR3 p.173) | . Astral attributes (SR3 p.173–174) . | Physical | While projecting | . | Strength | Charisma | . | Quickness | Intelligence | . | Body | Willpower | . | Reaction | Intelligence, and Initiative is INT + 20 + 1D6 | . Astral combat (SR3 p.174–175) . | Astral combat uses the melee rules. There are no ranged attacks except spells. | Perceiving is not projecting. A character who is astrally perceiving, such as an adept with Astral Perception, and other dual beings fight with their normal physical Attributes, skills and Combat Pool, and keep their normal Reaction and Initiative. The Astral Combat Pool below and the astral attributes above are for projecting characters only. (SR3 p.174) | A projecting character uses the Astral Combat Pool, (INT + WIL + CHA) ÷ 2. (SR3 p.44, p.174) Attack with an armed skill if you have a weapon focus, Unarmed Combat otherwise, or Sorcery in its place. | Damage: a projecting character deals unarmed (Charisma)M; armed, Charisma plus the weapon focus’s damage. An astrally perceiving character or other dual being deals (Strength)M, or its weapon’s own damage when armed. Spirits, foci and barriers deal (Force)M. (SR3 p.176) | Worn armor is useless on the astral. Natural armor, such as a troll’s or an adept’s Mystic Armor, still counts. (SR3 p.172, p.175) | The attacker picks Stun or Physical damage. Wounds appear on your physical body. If your astral form dies, your body dies. (SR3 p.175) | Wards and other astral barriers block astral movement, and the only way through is to beat the barrier in astral combat. (SR3 p.174) | .

3.title: 3. What a starting elven mage knows
3.content: The Awakened world . | The Awakening happened in 2011. On 24 December, passengers on a bullet train saw the great dragon Ryumyo appear near Mount Fuji. (SR3 p.25) | Traditions: mages treat magic as a discipline of formulae and elements. (SR3 p.158) Shamans follow a totem, which grants bonus dice for some spells and spirits and penalties for others. (SR3 p.163–165) | Essence and Magic: every full point of Essence lost, or fraction of one, costs a point of Magic. Cyberware is the usual cause. (SR3 p.160) | Magic and the law: in the UCAS and CAS, any spell, spirit or focus of Force 3 or higher is legally regulated, and permits are available. Killing with magic is treated as premeditated. (MitS p.11) | . Elven heritage . | Tír Tairngire, “the Land of Promise” (SR3 p.30), takes up most of the former state of Oregon plus parts of Washington and California. (SR3 p.321) | It’s ruled by the Council of Princes, with High Prince Lugh Surehand. The Council was all-elven at first; it later admitted other metahumans, including the dragon Lofwyr. (SR3 p.30) | Rumors of immortal elves who lived through the last low-magic age are not covered in the core rulebook. Treat them as street talk. | . Street survival . | The megacorps hold extraterritoriality: their ground, their law. (SR3 p.22) | Without a SIN you have few civil rights, but you’re also harder to trace. See SINs & the SINless. (SR3 p.238) | .

16.title: Action economy  (SR3 p.104–108)
16.content: In your Combat Phase you take either two Simple Actions or one Complex Action. (SR3 p.104) . Separately, you may take one Free Action during any character’s Combat Phase, including your own. You can’t take one before your first Combat Phase of the first Initiative Pass. Free Actions taken in someone else’s phase resolve last in that phase. (SR3 p.105) A Free Action can also be taken in place of a Simple Action. (SR3 p.105) . Free Actions (SR3 p.105) . Activate cyberware · call a shot · change a smartgun’s fire mode · deactivate a focus · delay an action · drop an object · drop prone · drop a sustained spell · eject a smartgun clip · gesture · observe (no Perception Test) · speak a word or short phrase · allocate Spell Defense dice. 17.title: Ranged combat  (SR3 p.109–114)
17.content: Attack Test ─▶ Dodge Test (optional) ─▶ Damage Resistance Test ─▶ Compare & stage . | Base target number from range: Short 4, Medium 5, Long 6, Extreme 9, using the band for your weapon on the Weapon Range Table. (SR3 p.111) Apply the modifiers below. | Attack Test: the ranged combat skill plus any Combat Pool dice. Count successes. No successes means a miss. (SR3 p.113) | Dodge Test (defender’s choice): Combat Pool dice only, against TN 4, plus 1 per 3 rounds of a burst or full-auto attack, plus 1 per meter of shotgun spread, plus the defender’s wound modifier. | Beat the attacker’s successes and the attack misses completely. A tie does not count. | Otherwise the dodge successes aren’t wasted. They add to your Damage Resistance successes. (SR3 p.113) | . | Damage Resistance Test: Body (including dermal armor) plus any Combat Pool dice left, against TN = weapon Power − armor, minimum 2. (SR3 p.113) | Determine the outcome: compare the attacker’s successes with the defender’s total (dodge + resistance). (SR3 p.113) . | Attacker ahead: stage the Damage Level up one step (L → M → S → D) per 2 successes over the defender’s total. | Defender ahead: stage it down one step per 2 successes over the attacker’s. Below Light, no damage. | Tie: base damage. | In ranged combat, staging stops at Deadly. Extra successes are discarded. (SR3 p.113) | . | . Worked example, from the rulebook (SR3 p.113) . Liam (Pistols 6) fires an Ares Predator (9M) and gets 5 successes. Snot (Body 5, ballistic armor 4, already Lightly wounded) dodges with all 5 Combat Pool dice against TN 5 (4, +1 for his wound) and gets 2. That’s not enough to dodge, but the 2 count. His Damage Resistance Test is 5 Body dice against TN 5 (9 − 4) and gets 1. Snot’s total is 3, Liam’s is . | Liam is 2 ahead, so the damage stages up once to 9S. | .

18.title: Melee combat  (SR3 p.120–123)
18.content: Melee is a Complex Action. It is an opposed test: both sides roll. (SR3 p.108, p.122) . | Attacker: combat skill plus Combat Pool dice against base TN 4, modified. (SR3 p.122) | Defender: the same, also against base TN 4, modified. (SR3 p.122) | Most successes hits. A tie goes to the attacker. (SR3 p.122) | The winner stages the damage up one level per 2 successes over the loser’s. In melee, once the level reaches Deadly, every 2 further successes add +1 Power. (SR3 p.122) | The loser rolls Body against Power − Impact armor. Every 2 successes reduce the Damage Level by one. (SR3 p.122) | . Reach gives a differential. The fighter with the longer reach may take the difference as a −TN to their own test or a +TN to the opponent’s. (SR3 p.121) .

29.title: Selling harvested chrome
29.content: Man & Machine has no separate resale rule for used implants, so sell them the same way as any other loot. Use the fencing rules (SR3 p.237–238): a 30% base, 5% per net success on the Negotiation, never below 10% or above 50%. Stolen chrome isn’t standard gear, so expect the Finding a Fence TN to rise. Example. A dead samurai’s smartlink (2,500¥) and retractable spur (11,500¥) (SR3 p.302) list at 14,000¥ together. The fence’s base offer is 4,200¥. Depending on the Negotiation, the deal can’t go below 1,400¥ or above 7,000¥. Optional flavor, not from the books. Tracking tags or corporate lockouts on stolen high-end implants, and a time limit for pulling chrome from a corpse, are good complications. If you use them, set the tests yourself; neither book gives numbers.

39.title: Getting on the Matrix
39.content: User Modes (MDF p.10) . Tortoise adds +2 TN to every Matrix test and cybercombat roll. Only VR-Hot gets true Matrix Initiative and benefits from Response — the other three run on whatever Initiative dice you’d roll in the meat world, full stop. (MDF p.10) . Skills (MDF p.11) . Four Intelligence-linked skills cover the Matrix: Computer (legitimate use — logons, moving around, ordinary prompts; defaults from Electronics), Hacking (illegal or scrutinized action, opposed by the target’s Sys/Sec; defaults from Computer), Cybercombat (fighting other icons; defaults from Computer), and Programming (writing or fixing utilities, skillsofts and agents; defaults from Computer). Hacking Pool (MDF p.11) . Hacking Pool = Intelligence + ⌊MPCP ÷ 3⌋. It behaves like any other dice pool (SR3 p.43): refreshes each Combat Turn, and you split it freely across Hacking, Cybercombat, or whatever else you’re rolling in the Matrix that turn. Response (MDF p.14) . Response on a deck is the Matrix’s version of wired reflexes: each point adds +2 Reaction and +1D6 Matrix Initiative, but only while you’re running VR-Hot. The GM can respond with any mix of: dumping the decker (triggering Dumpshock, below), leaking pieces of their session to the authorities (what their icon looked like, their handle, their gear, and roughly where they’re jacked in from), and sending a physical security response their way.

41.title: Cybercombat (MDF p.26)
41.content: Any icon can attack any other icon it can see sharing the same node or zone. Attacking automatically reveals your own icon if it wasn’t visible already. | Attacker rolls Cybercombat plus Hacking Pool against a base TN of 4, adjusted for circumstances. | Defender rolls the same way, same base TN. | Compare successes. Whoever has more hits their target — a tie favours the defender. | Stage the damage. The winner’s Damage Level rises one step for every two net successes; past Deadly, extra net successes add to Power instead. | Resist. The target rolls its System Rating (or MPCP) against a TN equal to the attack’s Power minus its own Security Threshold or Firewall — those numbers work as armour here. Every two successes drops the Damage Level by one. Utilities like Armor, Biofeedback Filtering, and Shield can chip in too. | . An icon’s own Matrix Condition Monitor is 10 boxes; filling it crashes the icon and — for a persona — dumps its user. Damage that overflows the user’s Matrix CM becomes real Biofeedback damage, Stun or Physical depending on their User Mode, the same split as Dumpshock below. (MDF p.26) . As it fills, the Matrix Condition Monitor penalises the icon’s tests the same way a character’s wounds do: +1 TN from the 1st box, +2 from the 3rd, +3 from the 6th, and +4 at the 10th. (MDF p.12) . Two more Matrix hazards worth knowing: a decker can permanently or temporarily disable a real-world Matrix device by finding its icon and crashing it in cybercombat, and an aggressive icon can Link-Lock a target so it can’t go hidden and needs a Willpower test just to log off cleanly — failing that test causes Dumpshock. (MDF p.27) .

42.title: Dumpshock (MDF p.27)
42.content: Getting yanked off the Matrix without a clean logoff hits you with Dumpshock: . | You immediately resist Serious biofeedback damage, with Power equal to the System Rating of whatever dumped you. | Tortoise and AR users don’t feel it at all. VR-Cold takes it as Stun; VR-Hot takes it as Physical. | You’re also rattled for the next 10 minutes — everything you do carries a +2 TN penalty until it wears off. | .

43.title: IC and Agents (MDF p.24, p.36)
43.content: IC (and Agents, which work the same way mechanically) come in three grades: . | White — nuisance-tier defenses. Can’t do more than Moderate damage to an icon, and can’t touch a decker’s real body at all. Every host can field it. | Gray — full cybercombat capability, and can permanently damage a decker’s actual deck (burn MPCP or utility slots). Still can’t reach the decker’s body directly. Needs the host’s Mainframe Support module. | Black — the only grade that can hurt the decker’s real body directly, and it’s legally allowed to. Also needs Mainframe Support. | . A sample of named agents from the book, by grade (MDF p.34): . | Grade | Examples | . | White | ARis, Authenticator, Crippler, Gemini, Looper, Mr. Medkit, Scrambler, Tracker | . | Gray | Blaster, Dataworm, Hydra, Killer, Tar Baby | . | Black | Ripper, Sparky | . Initiative for IC and Agents comes from the host’s Security Tier, not their own stats: . | Host Security Tier | Initiative | . | Ivory | Agent’s Rating | . | Blue | 1D6 + Agent’s Rating | . | Green | 2D6 + Agent’s Rating | . | Orange | 3D6 + Agent’s Rating | . | Red and above | 4D6 + Agent’s Rating | . (MDF p.36) Their Firewall equals their host’s Security Threshold — there’s no separate IC stat for it. Agents automatically know Computer and Cybercombat at their own Rating and share their host’s memory and active utilities.

Beyond programs, two other utility types exist: passcodes, which grant automatic, no-roll marks on whatever they’re keyed to, and protocols, unusual GM-defined applications (the book gives a few examples, like one that purges an infiltrating agent or one that buys a convergent decker extra time before the trace lands).

45.title: Doing it in The 2nd Chumming (Foundry)
45.content: Choosing the ruleset . A world setting, Matrix Ruleset (under Foundry’s Configure Settings), switches between “Matrix Defragged v2” (the default, described on this page) and “Orthodox SR3 Matrix”. Changing it needs a full Foundry restart, and the GM sees a warning that switching mid-campaign could break things — this is a session-zero decision, not a mid-run one. Getting on the Matrix . On the Matrix tab of a character or NPC sheet: . | User Mode buttons — TRM, AR, VR-Cold, VR-Hot — set your Matrix mode. Clicking one opens an “Enter Matrix” dialog to pick which host actor you’re connecting to; confirming sets both the mode and your active host. Clicking the same mode again disconnects you and drops you from that host’s roster. Switching into either VR mode while driving a vehicle in rigger-control mode automatically kicks the vehicle back to remote control, since the two are mutually exclusive. | Cyberdecks are items in your inventory. The Matrix tab lists yours (name, MPCP, Firewall, Response) with an Equip toggle. The equipped deck shows its full stat block — MPCP, Firewall, Response, memory used/total, free utility slots, transfer rate, Flux rating, your Hacking Pool bonus, and your Matrix Initiative — plus its own 10-box Matrix condition track. | Programs are also items; drag one onto a numbered utility slot on your deck to load it. A slot can be marked burned if an attack knocks it out, or ejected to swap the program out. Loaded programs are rolled straight from their slot (hold Shift for physical dice). | . Node tracking and prompts . While connected to a host, the Matrix tab shows which node you’re in, a Link-Locked flag, and your current marks as removable chips — plus a manual “add a mark” option for anything the GM rules outside the normal roll. Picking a node lists that node’s available prompts, each flagged for whether failing it raises Overwatch and whether succeeding grants a mark, with a one-click Use button that rolls it. Rolling a hacking action . A Hacking Action button (visible once you’re connected) opens a dialog pre-filled with your Hacking or Computer rating, your available Hacking Pool, the connected host, a default TN drawn from the host’s System Rating (plus any deck-damage or host-alert penalty already in effect), its Security Threshold, a field to allocate Hacking Pool dice, and a checkbox — on by default — to raise Overwatch automatically if you miss the threshold. Rolling it compares your successes to the threshold exactly as described above; falling short with that box checked posts an Overwatch warning against the host and bumps its tracked total by one. No Hacking or Computer skill at all routes you through the system’s usual Default Table first. Cybercombat . A Cybercombat button lets you target anyone sharing your host connection — other connected deckers, deployed IC, or agents — and posts a two-sided card for the exchange. Each side’s own half shows their skill, available Hacking Pool, TN, and damage code, editable only by that side; a GM-only resolve button settles things if someone goes AFK. Resolving the card charges each side’s Hacking Pool properly (both attacker and defender, through the same GM-routed pool spend used elsewhere in this system, so it works correctly even from a non-owning client) and rolls only the dice actually paid for. A degradable attack program used in the exchange loses a point of rating each time, and crashes outright once it would drop below 1. Dumpshock . A Dumpshock button (shown while in either VR mode) is a manual trigger for a GM or player to use whenever the fiction calls for an abrupt disconnection — a reboot, a cut connection, a power loss. It opens a small dialog to pick a connected host (which fills in Power from that host’s System Rating) or set Power by hand, then posts a Serious biofeedback announcement — Physical for VR-Hot, Stun for VR-Cold — with a resist button. As everywhere else in this system, the roll only announces the damage; the GM still clicks the wound boxes. Host sheets, Security Sheaf, and IC . A host is its own actor type with a dedicated sheet covering its node layout, its Security Sheaf, its I/O ports, and its roster of connected users and agents. The Security Sheaf tab sets the host’s Security Tier (which fills in the matching Threshold automatically) and shows its 10-box Overwatch track; the GM can seed a standard set of Trigger Steps, assign specific IC to each one, and deploy that IC into the current encounter when a step fires. IC and Agent actors get their own sheet type, tracking Rating, grade (White/Gray/Black), and their own Matrix condition track — an Agent additionally names the actor operating it, whose loaded attack program supplies its damage. Any IC flagged as deployed to a host becomes a valid cybercombat target for everyone connected there. Right now, only the first Overwatch trigger — a failed Hacking Test — raises the tracker automatically. Crashing an icon without Suppression, live Trigger Step countdowns, and the Suppression utility itself are still manual, GM-adjudicated calls from the Security Sheaf tab (tracked as open work, TODO 128).

46.title: Worked example
46.content: Voss decks with Intelligence 4 and a cyberdeck running MPCP 8, Firewall 4, Response 1, and Hacking 5. Her Hacking Pool is Intelligence 4 + ⌊8 ÷ 3⌋ = 4 + 2 = 6. She’s running VR-Hot, so her Matrix Initiative gets the Response bonus: +2 Reaction and one extra die on top of her usual 1D6. She jacks into a corporate research host: System Rating 7, Security Tier Red (Threshold 4). | First hack. She commits 3 Hacking Pool dice to her Hacking 5, rolling 8 dice against TN 7 (the host’s System Rating), and gets 5 successes. | Check the Threshold. 5 is at or above 4, so she succeeds and picks up a mark on the node she’s targeting. No Overwatch gained. | Second hack, pushing further in the same Combat Turn, committing her remaining 3 Hacking Pool dice: 8 dice against TN 7 nets her only 3 successes this time — short of the Red host’s Threshold 4. The hack fails, and her Overwatch on this host rises from 0 to 1. | If her Overwatch ever reached 10, Convergence would follow: the GM might trigger Dumpshock at Power 7 (the host’s System Rating) — Physical for her, since she’s in VR-Hot — leak pieces of her session, and send security to her jackpoint. | . If instead an IC engaged her in cybercombat: say a Gray IC (Rating 5) attacks. Both sides roll Cybercombat plus Hacking Pool against the base TN 4. If Voss nets 3 successes over the IC’s total, her attack utility’s Damage Level steps up once (two successes per step). The IC then resists with its own Rating against a TN equal to her attack’s Power minus its Firewall (its host’s Security Threshold — 4 here), soaking off Damage Levels two successes at a time.

47.title: Decking (SR3 core)
47.content: This page covers the core rulebook’s own Matrix chapter (SR3 p.199–232), plus the hot/cold ASIST rules from the Matrix sourcebook. This system calls this ruleset “Orthodox SR3 Matrix” to distinguish it from Matrix Defragged, a fan-made simplified ruleset this table can run instead — see Decking (Matrix Defragged) if that’s what your GM chose. The two rulesets are mechanically incompatible; this page only covers Orthodox. | The pieces . | Hacking Pool (SR3 p.207) | Matrix Initiative (SR3 p.209, p.223) | . | Hosts, grids, and getting in | Security tally, alerts, and the Security Sheaf (SR3 p.210–211) | System operations (SR3 p.214–219) | Cybercombat (SR3 p.222–224) | Intrusion Countermeasures (IC) (SR3 p.227–230) | Dump Shock (SR3 p.227) | Hot and Cold ASIST (Matrix p.18) | Doing it in The 2nd Chumming (Foundry) . | Choosing the ruleset | Deck and persona | Jacking in and running | System Tests and cybercombat | IC and the host sheet | Dumpshock | . | Worked example | .

48.title: The pieces
48.content: A decker’s cyberdeck defines everything about their persona in the Matrix. Its central number is the MPCP Rating — think of it as the deck’s overall processing muscle. Three times the MPCP Rating is the total the decker can spread across four persona programs: Bod, Evasion, Masking, and Sensor, none of which can individually exceed the MPCP itself. These four act as the persona’s “attributes” whenever something in the Matrix tests against the decker directly. (SR3 p.206) . A deck also carries Hardening, which blunts damage from the nastiest IC; Active and Storage Memory, which limit how many utility programs can run at once versus just be carried; an I/O Speed for moving data; and Response Increase, the Matrix’s answer to wired reflexes — each point adds +2 to Reaction and +1D6 to Matrix Initiative. A deck supports at most 3 points, and no more than its MPCP ÷ 4 (round down), so a deck of MPCP 3 or less can’t run any. (SR3 p.206–207) . Most ordinary Matrix users aren’t running a full cyberdeck at all — they’re on a cyberterminal (“tortoise” in decker slang), a cheaper, weaker rig capped at a low MPCP. The upside: tortoise users can’t be hurt by black IC or Dumpshock. (SR3 p.207–208) . Hacking Pool (SR3 p.207) . Hacking Pool = ⌊(Intelligence + deck MPCP) ÷ 3⌋. It works like any other dice pool and can help almost any Matrix test — logons, attacks, defenses, maneuvers — but it can’t be spent resisting damage from gray or black IC; only Karma Pool or the decker’s own enhancements help there. Matrix Initiative (SR3 p.209, p.223) . Outside combat, a decker’s number of actions per turn comes from their Reaction divided by 10 (rounded up), plus one extra action per bonus Initiative die from Response Increase. In cybercombat, it works like ordinary SR3 Initiative: base Reaction plus 1D6, with each point of Response Increase adding +2 Reaction and another die. Reflex boosts that only affect the physical body — wired reflexes, magic, vehicle rigs — don’t carry over into the Matrix. Staying in live voice or text contact with the outside world while decking costs a die of Initiative.

49.title: Hosts, grids, and getting in
49.content: Every host or grid carries an overall Security Rating — a colour code plus a number — and five subsystem ratings: Access, Control, Index, Files, and Slave. Each subsystem is the TN for a specific kind of illegitimate action against it: getting in at all uses Access, kicking a user off or reprogramming something uses Control, searching for data uses Index, reading or writing files uses Files, and operating a connected physical device (a camera, a maglock) uses Slave. (SR3 p.205–206) . The colour code — Blue (barely any security), Green (average), Orange (a system worth protecting), or Red (the kind that shoots first) — gives a rough sense of what to expect before a decker even rolls anything, and unofficially there’s a level above Red that deckers call “Ultra-Violet.” (SR3 p.205) . A System Test is always a Success Contest: the decker’s Computer skill (plus any Hacking Pool committed) against the relevant subsystem rating, opposed by the host’s own Security Value rolled against the decker’s Detection Factor — the average of their Masking Rating and any Sleaze utility they’re running (or half their Masking if they aren’t). Whoever nets more successes wins; a tie goes to the decker. (SR3 p.207, p.209–210) . Getting from grid to host works through System Access Nodes, and hosts can be arranged in different topologies — a simple open connection straight off a public grid, tiered behind a gatekeeper host, linked host-to-host, or tucked away on a private corporate grid entirely — which mostly changes what a decker has to fight through to reach the target. (SR3 p.203–204) .

50.title: Security tally, alerts, and the Security Sheaf (SR3 p.210–211)
50.content: Every success the host scores against a decker — win or lose the contest — adds to that decker’s running security tally on that system, for as long as they stay logged on. A security sheaf is the GM’s plan for what that tally triggers: a list of thresholds (“trigger steps”), each one arming some mix of IC and raising the system’s alert status. Systems start with no alert. Enough tally reaches a passive alert, which typically starts throwing proactive IC at the decker and adds +2 to every subsystem rating; enough more reaches an active alert, tightening things further. How dense the trigger steps are, and how much tally each one takes, is entirely the GM’s call — a high-security system stacks its triggers close together, a relaxed one spreads them out.

51.title: System operations (SR3 p.214–219)
51.content: Deckers act on a host through system operations — named commands with their own test, utility, and action type. Every one of them is really the same System Test underneath (Computer skill against a subsystem, opposed by the host’s Security Value against your Detection Factor); the operation just tells you which subsystem to use and how big an action it costs. | Operation | Subsystem tested | Helpful utility | Action | . | Analyze Host | Control | Analyze | Complex | . | Analyze IC | Control | Analyze | Free | . | Analyze Icon | Control | Analyze | Free | . | Analyze Security | Control | Analyze | Simple | . | Analyze Subsystem | Targeted subsystem | Analyze | Simple | . | Control Slave | Slave | Spoof | Complex | . | Decrypt Access | Access | Decrypt | Simple | . | Decrypt File | Files | Decrypt | Simple | . | Decrypt Slave | Slave | Decrypt | Simple | . | Download Data | Files | Read/Write | Simple | . | Edit File | Files | Read/Write | Simple | . | Edit Slave | Slave | Spoof | Complex | . | Graceful Logoff | Access | Deception | Complex | . | Locate Access Node | Index | Browse | Complex | . | Locate Decker | Index | Scanner | Complex | . | Locate File | Index | Browse | Complex | . | Locate IC | Index | Analyze | Complex | . | Locate Slave | Index | Browse | Complex | . | Logon to Host | Access | Deception | Complex | . | Logon to LTG | Access | Deception | Complex | . | Logon to RTG | Access | Deception | Complex | . | Make Comcall | Files | Commlink | Complex | . | Monitor Slave | Slave | Spoof | Simple | . | Null Operation | Control | Deception | Complex | . | Swap Memory | — | — | Simple | . | Tap Comcall | (special) | Commlink | Complex | . | Upload Data | Files | Read/Write | Simple | . A few in words: Logon to Host/LTG/RTG get you into a host or grid and start your security tally there. Locate operations are “interrogations” — you can repeat them, narrowing your search each time, to track down a file, a slave device, another decker, or IC. Download/Upload Data and Swap Memory move data or programs and take real time to finish, running in the background once started. Control Slave, Edit Slave, Monitor Slave, Make Comcall, and Tap Comcall are “monitored” operations — you spend a Free Action every Initiative Pass to keep them going, or they abort. Graceful Logoff is the clean way out, avoiding Dump Shock and wiping your tracks; jacking out any other way risks it.

52.title: Cybercombat (SR3 p.222–224)
52.content: Cybercombat runs on the same bones as ordinary SR3 combat — roll Initiative, then act in order — just compressed into 3-second Combat Turns like everywhere else. A few Matrix-specific wrinkles: . | An icon has to be visible or located before you can attack it. Attacking automatically makes your own icon visible unless you pull off a maneuver to hide it. | Attacks are Simple Actions, rolled with an offensive utility program (plus any Hacking Pool) against a target number set by whether the target is Legitimate or an Intruder and by the host’s security code: . | Host security code | TN to hit an Intruding icon | TN to hit a Legitimate icon | . | Blue | 6 | 3 | . | Green | 5 | 4 | . | Orange | 4 | 5 | . | Red | 3 | 6 | . A hotter host makes its own defenders easier to hit and intruders harder — the numbers flip depending which side of the law your target is on. (SR3 p.224) . | Net successes stage damage exactly like a firearm hit: two successes per step up for the attacker, two per step down for the defender’s resistance roll (made with the icon’s Bod Rating, or the host’s Security Value for an IC program). | Icons only have one condition track — no separate Stun — and filling all 10 boxes crashes the icon. For a decker’s persona, that means getting dumped from the Matrix (and risking Dumpshock, below); it doesn’t disconnect them if black IC did it — it just makes frying their brain that much easier. | Simsense overload: getting hit by white or gray IC can bleed a little Stun damage into the decker’s real body through the ASIST link. A failed Willpower test against a TN set by how badly the icon was hurt means a light Stun wound. | . Utility programs round the picture out on both sides: things like Armor (soaks incoming damage), Cloak and Lock-On (help or hurt evasive maneuvers), and Medic (patches an icon back up) all work by adding or subtracting their own rating from the relevant roll — check each utility’s own write-up for the exact math.

53.title: Intrusion Countermeasures (IC) (SR3 p.227–230)
53.content: IC comes in three grades: . | Grade | Can reach | Named examples | . | White | Only the decker’s on-line icon — attribute damage, dumping, or scrambled data | Cripplers, Killer, Probe, Scramble, Tar Baby | . | Gray | The decker’s actual cyberdeck and utilities, permanently, on top of cybercombat | Blaster, Ripper, Sparky, Tar Pit | . | Black | The decker’s real body, directly and legally | Lethal and non-lethal black IC | . Killer IC’s damage stages off its Rating, with the Damage Level set by the host’s own security code: . | Host security code | IC Damage Level | . | Blue | Moderate | . | Green | Moderate | . | Orange | Serious | . | Red | Serious | . (SR3 p.224) . Facing lethal black IC means resisting with Body (Hardening helps; Hacking Pool doesn’t — only Karma Pool or the decker’s own enhancements can help here), and getting free of it after being hit takes a Complex Action and a Willpower test against the IC’s own Rating. An IC program’s own Initiative scales with the host’s security code, not any stat of its own: . | Host security code | IC Initiative | . | Blue | 1D6 + IC Rating | . | Green | 2D6 + IC Rating | . | Orange | 3D6 + IC Rating | . | Red | 4D6 + IC Rating | . (SR3 p.223) . Tortoise (cyberterminal) users are entirely immune to black IC and Dumpshock, which is part of why they’re the safer — if slower — way to touch the Matrix.

54.title: Dump Shock (SR3 p.227)
54.content: Getting crashed off the Matrix, or jacking out without a clean logoff, risks Dump Shock: Stun damage with Power equal to the host’s Security Value, and a Damage Level set by the host’s security code: . | Host security code | Dump Shock Damage Level | . | Blue | Light | . | Green | Moderate | . | Orange | Serious | . | Red | Deadly | . Also worth knowing: getting hit by white or gray IC risks a little simsense bleed-through even before any of that — a Willpower test against a fairly low TN (2 for Light icon damage, 3 for Moderate, 5 for Serious) keeps it off, and failing means a single light Stun wound. There’s no TN for Deadly icon damage, because taking Deadly damage crashes the icon outright and exposes its user to Dump Shock instead. (SR3 p.226–227) .

55.title: Hot and Cold ASIST (Matrix p.18)
55.content: How a decker’s cyberdeck talks to their brain matters: . | Cold ASIST is the standard, legal interface — the kind that ships on cyberterminals and most decks. It caps the intensity of the simsense feed, which means it can’t be pushed to lethal levels: black IC that would otherwise deal lethal damage is treated as non-lethal against a cold ASIST user. | Hot ASIST cranks that ceiling off. It’s what actually lets a decker take advantage of Response Increase and Hacking Pool in the first place, and it enables an extra speed bonus for running fully hands-free (“pure DNI”). The price is that black IC becomes genuinely lethal against a hot ASIST user, and — as if that weren’t enough — hot ASIST interfaces are illegal in their own right. | .

56.title: Doing it in The 2nd Chumming (Foundry)
56.content: Choosing the ruleset . A world setting, Matrix Ruleset (in Foundry’s Configure Settings), switches between “Matrix Defragged v2” (the default) and “Orthodox SR3 Matrix” — this page’s rules. Changing it needs a full Foundry restart, and the GM sees a warning that switching mid-campaign could break things, so it’s a session-zero decision. Deck and persona . On a character or NPC’s Matrix tab under the Orthodox ruleset, your cyberdeck’s stats live directly on your sheet rather than as a separate item: Model, MPCP, Hardening, Active/Storage Memory, I/O Speed, and Response (Response Increase). A Browse Cyberdecks button opens a picker over the system’s cyberdeck compendium and loads a chosen model’s stats onto your sheet in one click. Your four persona programs — Bod, Evasion, Masking, Sensor — are editable fields the sheet checks against your MPCP: it flags a warning if any single program exceeds MPCP, or if they add up past three times MPCP. A Sleaze rating field and a Loaded Programs list (each with its own rating and computed memory cost, filled from a similar Browse Programs picker) round out your utilities. The sheet computes your Hacking Pool, Detection Factor, and Matrix Initiative for you from these numbers. Jacking in and running . A Log On To Host control picks which host actor you’re connected to (and resets your security tally and alert level when you log on or off), and separate buttons set the host’s alert level — No Alert, Passive Alert, or Active Alert. A Matrix Condition Monitor — 10 clickable boxes, plus quick buttons for Light/Moderate/Serious/Deadly damage or healing one box — tracks your icon’s health; filling it triggers Dumpshock automatically: Stun, Power equal to the connected host’s Security Value, and a level from its Security Code (see Dump Shock above). System Tests and cybercombat . A System Test button opens a dialog naming the connected host, your Computer skill and Hacking Pool, your Detection Factor, and a dropdown to pick which subsystem — Access, Control, Index, Files, or Slave — the action uses; each option shows that subsystem’s rating (raised automatically if the host is on Passive Alert), and you can name the action and adjust the TN for any utility you’re running. Rolling it posts a two-sided chat card — your dice and TN on one side, the host’s Security Value and Detection Factor TN on the other — that resolves as a Success Contest exactly as described above. Any hits the host scores add straight to your tracked security tally, regardless of who wins the overall contest. A Cybercombat button works the same way against IC deployed on the connected host, posting its own two-sided card for the exchange. IC and the host sheet . A host actor under this ruleset sets its Security Code (Blue/Green/Orange/Red/Black) and Alert level (Passive/Active/Shutdown) at the top of its sheet, with its five subsystem ratings and overall Security Value editable below. Its IC tab lists IC actors assigned to it — each with a type drawn from a fixed roster of classic IC names, a Proactive/Reactive toggle, and a note for which alert level deploys it — and a deploy button that brings assigned IC into the current encounter. An IC actor’s own sheet is mostly just a Rating; its attack pool and the damage it can absorb both draw from its host’s Security Value rather than from any stat of its own, matching the book’s treatment of IC as an extension of the host defending it. Dumpshock . Beyond the automatic trigger when your Matrix Condition Monitor fills, a Dumpshock button on the Matrix tab lets a GM or player fire it manually for any other reason the story calls for. Its dialog takes the host’s Security Code and Security Value (filled in from the connected host) and posts the book’s damage: Stun, Power equal to the Security Value, and a level from the Dump Shock Damage Levels table (Blue Light, Green Moderate, Orange Serious, Red Deadly) — the same as the automatic version. The resist card rolls Willpower with no armor (a house ruling: the book names no attribute). Either way, the system only announces the damage; the GM still applies it. Hardening is tracked on the sheet and its tooltip describes the book’s effect, but nothing in this system’s dice-rolling code currently reads that field — it doesn’t yet reduce black IC damage or raise gray IC’s attack TN the way SR3 p.206 describes. Treat it as informational until that’s wired up.

57.title: Worked example
57.content: Delgado runs a deck with MPCP 6, split Bod 5 / Evasion 6 / Masking 4 / Sensor 3 (18 points total — right at 3× his MPCP), and Computer 5. His Intelligence is 4, so his Hacking Pool is ⌊(4 + 6) ÷ 3⌋ = 3. Running a Sleaze-5 utility, his Detection Factor is ⌈(4 + 5) ÷ 2⌉ = 5. He’s hitting a Green host with an Access Rating of 8, running a Decryption-3 utility to soften the target number. | Logon. He rolls Computer 5 plus 2 Hacking Pool dice (saving 1 for later) = 7 dice against a TN of 8 − 3 (his Decryption utility) = 5. He nets 3 successes. | The host resists. The GM rolls the host’s Security Value (say, 6 dice for this Green system) against Delgado’s Detection Factor of 5, and gets 1 success. | Result. 3 beats 1, so Delgado logs on cleanly. The host’s 1 success still adds to his security tally on this system — a small price for getting in. | Later, Delgado trips a Trigger Step and a Killer IC (Rating 6) attacks him in cybercombat. Its Attack Test nets 4 successes against his Evasion-based defense of 2 successes — 2 net successes, enough to step its damage up one level. Since this is a Green host, Killer IC there deals Moderate damage before staging, so Delgado is now facing Serious damage, resisted with his Bod Rating against the attack’s Power. | If that hit had crashed his icon instead, Delgado would be dumped and would need to resist Dump Shock — Stun damage at a Power equal to the host’s Security Value, with a Damage Level set by the host’s Green security code. | .

58.title: Drones
58.content: Running unmanned vehicles from a remote-control deck: jumping into one drone or sitting in the captain’s chair, the network and its subscriber list, the actions a rigger can take, giving a drone orders, and the drones in the core rulebook. 59.title: What makes a drone  (SR3 p.154, p.306)
59.content: A drone is any unmanned vehicle that can be run over a rigger network, from a matchbox-sized car to a modified sports car. 60.title: Jumped in, or the captain’s chair  (SR3 p.154)
60.content: Every drone affiliated with the rigger’s deck runs in one of two modes, and the rigger runs the whole network in one of two ways. |   | How it works | Dice | . | Primary drone | The rigger jumps in: controls it as if jacked directly into it. Only one at a time. | The rigger’s skills, plus Combat and Control Pool, and every rigger bonus. | . | Secondary drones | Everything else on the network. | The drone’s Pilot Rating in place of skill or Attribute. The book’s example (SR3 p.154): Rigger X is in the captain’s chair with three drones when a security transport closes in. 61.title: The remote-control network  (SR3 p.154–156)
61.content: A remote-control (RC) deck is the control station, and drones connect to it by radio on three channels: command (movement, actions and information), simsense (sight, sound and simsense) and system (network integrity and drone status). Subscriber lists (SR3 p.156) . | The deck only talks to drones on its subscriber list, which keeps intruders out. | The list holds twice the deck’s rating in drones; the deck can actively control as many as its rating. | A drone under the deck’s control is affiliated; the rigger can see through and command it, and it can talk to the other affiliated drones. A non-affiliated drone acts on its own, cut off from the network. | Affiliating or disaffiliating a drone is a Simple Action, so swapping one drone for another takes two Simple Actions or one Complex Action. A drone can’t act in the Combat Turn it’s affiliated. | . The book’s example (SR3 p.156): Josie’s Rating 4 deck holds up to 8 drones on its list but controls 4 at once. She has 6 listed and 4 affiliated. To bring in a ground patrol vehicle she spends one Simple Action dropping her surveillance drone and another adding the GPV, which can act from her next Combat Turn. Range (SR3 p.136–137) . Each success heals one box, up to the spell’s Force. Heal has no +2 penalty after an hour. | Natural healing uses the Healing Table (TN 4 / 6 / 8 / 10), and the base time is divided by your successes. The “nurse / hospital / DocWagon” modifiers in the original were invented. The real ones are on the Doctoring Table below. | The fourth level is Deadly, not “Lethal”. | .

The order matters for two reasons. First aid can’t help once magical healing has been applied, so do first aid first. And first aid and magic both have to happen before the “need a doctor?” test. (SR3 p.127, p.129) .

87.title: Step 0: The wound  (SR3 p.125–126)
87.content: Physical and Stun each have 10 boxes. The Light / Moderate / Serious / Deadly thresholds are 1 / 3 / 6 / 10 boxes, and they add +1 / +2 / +3 to target numbers and −1 / −2 / −3 to Initiative. At 10 boxes you’re unconscious. | Stun past 10 boxes spills into the Physical track, and you’re knocked out. | Physical past 10 boxes: you can survive overflow up to your Body rating. Until someone stabilizes you, you take another box every (Body) Combat Turns. Past Body in overflow, you’re dead. | . See Actions & Combat for the full table.

88.title: Step 1: Stabilize a dying character  (SR3 p.129)
88.content: Only for a Deadly wound. First aid can stabilize a Deadly wound but can’t reduce it. | Medic rolls Biotech against TN 10, with the modifiers from the First Aid Table in step 2. One success stabilizes the patient: the extra box every (Body) Combat Turns stops. | If that fails, the patient rolls natural Body against TN 10. With a success they stabilize on their own. If that fails too, they die once the damage exceeds their Body rating. | Trauma patch (optional, last resort): the patient gets an extra Body Test to stabilize, against TN 4 + the rating of any dermal armor or blood filters. Success stops the overflow damage. It makes permanent damage more likely: +2 to the step 4 test. | When professional help arrives, such as a hospital or a DocWagon paramedic with better Biotech, it makes another Biotech Test and Body Test. | .

91.title: Step 4: Deadly-wound aftermath  (SR3 p.127–129)
91.content: Only after a Deadly wound. Permanent damage. The patient rolls Body against TN 4. Dermal armor counts for this test, and use of a trauma patch adds +2. (SR3 p.127–128) . | Successes | Result | . | 0 | A vital organ or system is gravely damaged. The patient needs continuous care from someone with Biotech, the whole healing time doubles, and a transplant is needed. Roll 1D6 for the attribute permanently lost: 1 Body, 2 Strength, 3 Quickness, 4 Intelligence, 5 Willpower, 6 Reaction. | . | 1 | An eye or limb is lost and must be replaced, either natural or cyber. Base healing time +50%. Roll 1D6: 1 right arm, 2 left arm, 3 right leg, 4 left leg, 5 an ear, 6 an eye. | . | 2+ | No lasting damage. | . Magic loss. An Awakened patient with a Deadly wound rolls 2D6. At or below their Magic, they permanently lose 1 point. If the Deadly wound was also treated without the +2 Awakened modifier, they roll twice. (SR3 p.129) .

92.title: Step 5: Do you need a doctor?  (SR3 p.126–127)
92.content: Once first aid and magic are done, the patient makes a Body Test (natural Body, no cyberware) against the TN for their current wound: . | Wound level | TN | . | Light | 2 | . | Moderate | 4 | . | Serious | 6 | . | Deadly | Always needs medical attention | . | Any successes: you’ll heal without medical attention. | No successes: you won’t heal at all until you get medical attention, meaning a doctor, clinic or hospital. | . You can make this test any time, but doing it in combat costs your whole next Combat Turn. (SR3 p.126) .

93.title: Step 6: Heal over time  (SR3 p.127–128)
93.content: Physical damage heals one Damage Level at a time: Deadly to Serious, Serious to Moderate, and so on. When a level heals, the track drops to the lowest box of the next level. A Serious wound that heals to Moderate leaves exactly 3 boxes filled. For each level: . | The patient rolls Body against the TN on the Healing Table below. Add Doctoring Table modifiers if a doctor is involved. | Base time ÷ successes = how long that level takes to heal. It can never be shorter than the minimum time. | When the level heals, repeat for the next level down. | . Use this when a real doctor is looking after the patient. | Situation | Modifier | . | Intensive care (hospital only) | −2 | . | Long-term magical care | −2 | . | Conditions (apply only one): |   | . | Not in a hospital or clinic | +2 | . | Bad conditions | +3 | . | Terrible conditions | +4 | . | Patient is a magician | +2 | . | Patient’s natural Body 1–3 / 4–6 / 7–9 / 10+ | +0 / −1 / −2 / −3 | . | Patient’s natural Willpower 1–3 / 4–6 / 7–9 / 10+ | +0 / −1 / −2 / −3 | . What it costs (SR3 p.128) . | Service | Deadly | Serious | Moderate | Light | . | Paramedic first aid | 400¥ | 200¥ | 100¥ | 50¥ | . | Doctor’s services, per day | 400¥ | 200¥ | 100¥ | 50¥ | . A hospitalization lifestyle is 500¥ a day, including the doctor. Intensive care, for Deadly wounds only, is 1,000¥ a day.

94.title: Stun damage  (SR3 p.126)
94.content: Stun runs on its own track and recovers much faster. No medicine or known spell helps; you just rest. | The patient rolls Body or Willpower, whichever is higher, against TN 2, plus current Stun and Physical injury modifiers. | Recovering one box takes 60 minutes ÷ successes. Erase the box, then roll again for the next one. | The patient must be resting completely. If they’re interrupted, they start over, and the new roll can’t beat the first one. | . A character knocked out by Deadly Stun doesn’t wake up until the Stun is back down to Serious. Stim patches only mask Stun, at a price. (SR3 p.126, p.305) .

95.title: Worked example
95.content: Snot takes a Serious Physical wound (6 boxes) from a Predator. | Stabilize: not needed; it isn’t Deadly. | First aid, within the hour. Teammate Doc has Biotech 4 and a medkit, and it’s a city street (+1). The TN is 8 + 1 = 9, less 1 for Snot’s Body 5 = 8. Doc gets 1 success: the wound drops to Moderate (3 boxes). Treatment takes 15 ÷ 1 = 15 Combat Turns. | Magic. The team mage casts Treat, still within the hour, against 10 − Snot’s Essence 6 = TN 4, and gets 2 successes. Two boxes heal, leaving 1 box: Light. Drain is resisted at Moderate, Snot’s wound level when the spell was cast. Nobody can use first aid or healing magic on this wound again. | Aftermath: not needed; it wasn’t Deadly. | Need a doctor? Snot rolls Body 5 against TN 2 for a Light wound and succeeds. He’ll heal on his own. | Heal over time. Body 5 against TN 4 gets 2 successes: 24 hours ÷ 2 = 12 hours, above the 2-hour minimum. He needs at least a Low lifestyle for that time. | .

98.title: The house-rule framework
98.content: The specialist pages use this structure. It came from the original gists. The numbers are not from any SR3 book, and are much higher than the Companion’s baselines. For example, a “professional” bodyguard at 1,500¥ a night compares with the book’s 200¥ a day. They fit a high-paying campaign. Scale them to your table. Fee = base day rate × threat multiplier, plus hazard pay (a percentage of that), plus expenses. | Base day rate is set by the specialist’s tier in their main skill (1–3, 4–5, 6–7, 8+). | Threat multiplier, from about ×1 for routine work to ×3–×6 for heavy opposition. | Hazard pay for being on-site rather than working remotely, usually +50% to +100%. | Expenses and deposits: ammunition, reagents, fake IDs, drone and deck repairs. By the book, Johnson covers expenses only if they’re negotiated (MJLBB p.20–21). | . Fixers take a finder’s fee, which the books don’t quantify. The original gists suggested 10–30% depending on how rare the specialist is. Many top-tier freelancers will ask instead for an equal share of the team’s payout. 103.title: The Sixth World: who runs it
103.content: The megacorporations, the syndicates, the policlubs, the governments and the dragons, and how they deal with each other. That web of rivalries is where shadowruns come from. | The players at a glance | How the corps got above the law (SR3 p.22) | The Corporate Court: the referee | How the factions deal with each other . | Corp against corp: the shadow war | Corps in one city: the United Corporate Council (NS p.83) | Corps and syndicates | Corps and governments | Policlubs and everyone | The dragons | . | Using this at the table | . When this describes. These pages describe the world as of October 2059. The SR3 core book and New Seattle carry the story on into 2060; gamemasters will find those later events in the system’s GM Only compendium. Much of New Seattle is written as posts by shadowrunners on the Shadowland BBS, so it’s rumor as much as fact. These pages say “runners claim” or “rumor” when the book does. Anything stated as fact here is stated as fact in the book.

104.title: The players at a glance
104.content: | Faction | What it wants | Where to read more | . | Megacorporations | Profit, market share, and an edge over every rival. Each one is a law unto itself. | Megacorporations | . | The Corporate Court | Stability for the biggest corps: it settles disputes between them and acts for them together. | Below | . | Crime syndicates: Mafia, Yakuza, Triads, Seoulpa Rings | The shadow economy, meaning smuggling, vice, protection and fencing, and territory. | The Underworld | . | Policlubs (Humanis, ORC, the Empowerment Coalition) | Political causes. Some have terrorist groups fronting for them. | Politics, Police & Policlubs | . | Security corporations (Lone Star, Knight Errant) | Police contracts. Law enforcement is a business now. | Politics, Police & Policlubs | . | Nations (UCAS, NAN, Aztlan, Tir Tairngire, Japan…) | Borders and trade, and keeping the corps at arm’s length while needing their money. | Politics, Police & Policlubs | . | Dragons and the Draco Foundation | Their own goals. Lofwyr owns Saeder-Krupp, and Dunkelzahn’s will is still reshaping the world. | Megacorporations | .

105.title: How the corps got above the law  (SR3 p.22)
105.content: Two US Supreme Court rulings at the turn of the century made the modern megacorp: . | The Seretech decision upheld a corporation’s right to keep an armed force to protect its people and property. That legitimised private corporate armies. | The Shiawase decision established corporate extraterritoriality: a multinational gets the same rights and privileges as a foreign government. Its land is effectively foreign soil. | . The rest follows from those two rulings. A corp facility is a sovereign enclave with its own army, so the police can’t simply walk in, and no government can easily make a corp answer for anything. The SR3 introduction sums up the result. Megacorps are “a law unto themselves”, the nuyen is the world’s currency, and when a corp wants a job done without dirtying its hands, it hires shadowrunners (SR3 p.8).

106.title: The Corporate Court: the referee
106.content: The biggest corps answer, loosely, to one body: the Corporate Court, which they sit on themselves. | It owns the bank. In 2032–33 the Court took over Global Financial Services, which had replaced the World Bank. It moved GFS into orbit as the Zurich-Orbital Gemeinschaft Bank (SR3 p.31). | It acts for the corps together. In 2048 Aztlan nationalised every foreign business. The corps answered with Operation Reciprocity, a combined corporate military strike on Aztechnology troops in Ensenada. The Veracruz Settlement that followed compensated the other corps and let them back into Aztlan, provided Aztlan citizens held the major shares of their local subsidiaries. The same year, the Panama Canal became a Pan-Corporate Zone under the Court’s authority (SR3 p.31). | A seat on it is fiercely contested. Yamatetsu spent 2041 fighting for a seat on the Court and on the Zurich-Orbital board. When it won, the “Big Seven” became the Big Eight (SR3 p.31). In 2059 suborbital Flight 1118 from Tokyo crashed into the Redmond Barrens, killing Fuchi’s Court representative, David Hague. His seat went not to a Big Eight corp but to Wuxing, a family corp made rich by Dunkelzahn’s will (SR3 p.35). | . What that means for runners: the Court keeps corp-on-corp fighting deniable. An open war risks the others ganging up on you, as they did on Aztlan. A shadowrun that nobody can trace doesn’t.

107.title: How the factions deal with each other
107.content: Corp against corp: the shadow war . | Deniable assets. A corporate Mr. Johnson is paid from black-ops accounts, keeps his employer secret, and knows he’ll be disowned if he’s exposed (MJLBB p.17–18). Corporate Johnsons are the most common kind (MJLBB p.17). | Raids on rivals’ people and research. The defining fight of the moment is Fuchi against Renraku (SR3 p.34–35): . | In 2058, Dunkelzahn’s will gave Fuchi’s security chief, Miles Lanier, a seat on Renraku’s board, and he left Fuchi for Renraku. Months later, Renraku began producing remarkable technological advances. | Fuchi was already split into three internal factions, and the infighting got worse. | Around mid-2059, Fuchi formally accused Renraku of industrial espionage with Lanier’s help. The charges were dropped, but Lanier left Renraku and sold his Renraku stock to the Zurich-Orbital bank. | At about the same time, Richard Villiers of Fuchi formed Novatech and began quietly buying up his Fuchi North America holdings through it, expecting the rival factions to force him out. He offered Lanier the job of head of security. | . | Keeping newcomers out. The Big Eight work to crush smaller corps that Dunkelzahn’s will made rich, “with much resulting business for shadowrunners”. Lucien Cross of Cross Applied Technologies survived three assassination attempts in 2058 alone (SR3 p.35). | Infighting within a corp. Most corps fight themselves as well. Shiawase’s divisions compete for head-office money, and some of that rivalry ends in shadowruns (NS p.95). The Telestrian family is split into factions (NS p.88). Yamatetsu’s traditionalists resist its new ork chairman (SR3 p.35; NS p.96). | . Corps in one city: the United Corporate Council (NS p.83) . Seattle’s corps present one face to the city government through the United Corporate Council. It’s an advisory body to the governor that pushes the corporate agenda. It was formed in 2030, after a corp war in which Aztechnology wiped out Campana & Carrindum, so that such “misunderstandings” wouldn’t happen again. New Seattle calls it a small-scale version of the Corporate Court. Its members include the megacorps, the big local corps, Lone Star and the Draco Foundation. The backstabbing inside it is constant but subtle. A member that moves too openly risks the rest ganging up on it, so they hire runners for paydata, to give their lobbyists an edge. Corps and syndicates . | Hired muscle. Mitsuhama calls on the Seattle yakuza for its “special problems” (NS p.92–93). | The yakuza inside the boardroom. The yakuza’s sokaiya branch combines stock purchases with blackmail to steer corporations and skim their money (NS p.102). | The Triads and the Pacific Prosperity Group. Wuxing is the driving force behind the PPG, a trade bloc against Japanese economic dominance. Runners claim the Triads will target Wuxing’s rivals, Mitsuhama above all (NS p.96). | . Corps and governments . | Contracts are power. Seattle’s power grid, telecommunications, public databases and traffic grid are all run by corporations under contract (NS p.76). So are its police (NS p.76). | States own corps too. Gaeatronics is owned by the Salish-Shidhe Council (NS p.84). Telestrian Industries is “the Tir government’s proxy in Seattle”, runners claim, because the Council of Princes owns 5% of it (NS p.87–88). | Governments ban corps. Aztechnology is barred from doing business in California and Tir Tairngire (NS p.81, p.90), and so is Saeder-Krupp (NS p.95). Both run their interests there through shells and watchers based in Seattle. | And corps run cities. New York was rebuilt by the corps in exchange for concessions that leave them running it. Los Angeles’s leaders “dance to corporate hymns” (SR3 p.30). | . Policlubs and everyone . Policlubs keep their hands clean by funding terrorists. Humanis quietly pays groups like Alamos 20,000 to do the violence it publicly denies (NS p.79). Runners claim ORC leaders pass resources to pro-Awakened terror groups (NS p.80). Both have rich backers. Kenneth Brackhaven, a corporate investor and Humanis leader Karl Brackhaven’s nephew, has paid for the campaigns of at least six district mayors (NS p.83–84). See Politics, Police & Policlubs. The dragons . | Lofwyr announced in 2037 that he owned 63% of the company that became Saeder-Krupp, and made himself its chief executive (SR3 p.31). | Dunkelzahn was elected UCAS president and assassinated on his inauguration night. His will founded the Draco Foundation, and its individual bequests started trouble everywhere: it was “a master stroke of manipulation from beyond the grave” (SR3 p.34). | Runners speculate that the great dragons Lung and Ryumyo are playing a chess game along the Pacific Rim (NS p.104). It’s rumor, but it’s useful for a GM. | .

108.title: Using this at the table
108.content: These are suggestions, not rules. | Ask who gains. Most runs in these books trace back to one faction hurting another. Before a run, decide who the Johnson really works for, which rival is the real target, and who else is watching. The Johnson types are covered in (MJLBB p.17–18). | Use the rivalries listed above. Fuchi against Renraku, Fuchi’s three factions against each other (and Villiers’s new Novatech), the Seattle Mafia’s fight over who succeeds O’Malley, and Humanis against the Empowerment Coalition are all open in late 2059, and each one hires runners. | Expect retaliation. Mitsuhama, runners say, “makes examples of runners who double-cross them” (NS p.93). Cross Corp tags intruding deckers and comes to collect favours weeks later (NS p.91). | .

120.title: How to Initiate
120.content: How an Awakened character climbs the grades of initiation: what it costs, the ordeals that make it cheaper, magical groups, metamagic, and the geasa that keep a magician’s power when Magic is lost. Initiation isn’t in the core rulebook; all of this is from Magic in the Shadows (MitS p.30–33, p.57–79). | Who can initiate (MitS p.57–58) | What each grade gives (MitS p.58) | The Karma cost (MitS p.58) | Ordeals (MitS p.58–61) | Magical groups (MitS p.61–65) . | Strictures (MitS p.62–63) | . | Metamagic (MitS p.69–79) . | Learning a technique (MitS p.69–70) | Centering (MitS p.72–74) | . | Geasa (MitS p.30–33) | Doing it in The 2nd Chumming (Foundry) | .

121.title: Who can initiate  (MitS p.57–58)
121.content: Only the Awakened: full magicians, aspected magicians and adepts. A character can initiate alone or as a member of a magical group, which makes it cheaper. Each initiation adds a grade: the first makes you a Grade 1 initiate, the second Grade 2, and so on. The gamemaster decides when a character can initiate, and some time should pass between having the Karma and taking the next grade. They also decide what the process involves, guided by the character’s path: study, practice, rituals, or proving themselves (MitS p.57–58).

122.title: What each grade gives  (MitS p.58)
122.content: Every initiate gets these with each grade: . | Astral Reaction goes up by the grade. | An Astral Pool of dice equal to the grade. It can be used on any test on the astral plane or the metaplanes, including Astral Combat (even with Sorcery) and Astral Perception, except Magical Skill Tests. It refreshes like other pools. | A full magician’s first initiation opens the metaplanes of astral space (p.91). | . Then choose one of these three, each time: . | Option | Magic | And | . | Learn a metamagical technique | +1 | One technique you qualify for. Below. | . | Alter your astral signature | +1 | A Magic Test against 6 + the new grade, with no dice but Karma. Two or more successes change it. Each failure adds +1 to later attempts. | . | Shed a geas | none | One geas comes off a Magic point you already have, so that point works without it. Geasa. | . | Magic can rise above 6 this way. | Adepts get a Power Point for each point of Magic gained. See Physical Adepts. | . The book’s example (MitS p.58): Bandi, Magic 8, initiates to Grade 3 and tries to alter her signature. She rolls 8 dice against 6 + 3 = TN 9 and gets 1 success, which isn’t enough. Next time her TN is one higher.

123.title: The Karma cost  (MitS p.58)
123.content: Base cost = 5 + the grade you’re initiating to. Multiply by the initiation type, and round down. | Initiation Cost Table (MitS p.58) | Cost | . | Self-initiation | Base Cost × 3 | . | Self-initiation with an ordeal | Base Cost × 2.5 | . | Group initiation | Base Cost × 2 | . | Group initiation with an ordeal | Base Cost × 1.5 | . The same table worked out for the first six grades: . | Grade | Base | Self | Self + ordeal | Group | Group + ordeal | . | 1 | 6 | 18 | 15 | 12 | 9 | . | 2 | 7 | 21 | 17 | 14 | 10 | . | 3 | 8 | 24 | 20 | 16 | 12 | . | 4 | 9 | 27 | 22 | 18 | 13 | . | 5 | 10 | 30 | 25 | 20 | 15 | . | 6 | 11 | 33 | 27 | 22 | 16 | . The book’s example (MitS p.58): Eli, an owl shaman, initiates alone. Grade 1 costs (5 + 1) × 3 = 18, or 15 with an ordeal. Grade 2 costs 7 × 3 = 21, or 7 × 2.5 = 17.5, rounded down to 17, with an ordeal. In a group he’d have paid 6 × 2 = 12 for Grade 1, or 6 × 1.5 = 9 with an ordeal, and 14, or 10 with an ordeal, for Grade 2.

124.title: Ordeals  (MitS p.58–61)
124.content: An ordeal is a test of the candidate. It lowers the cost multiplier by 0.5. Choose it before initiating; only a deed can be done ahead of time. Pass it and you gain the grade. Fail and you try again, without paying the Karma a second time. An ordeal can be repeated only with the GM’s permission, and an oath never. | Ordeal | What it takes | . | Astral quest | A quest on the metaplanes with a rating of twice the grade. Shamans go to their totem’s metaplane, mages to each of the four elemental metaplanes. You must be able to project. After a failure, a Willpower Test against the grade sets the preparation time: 10 days divided by the successes. | . | Asceticism | Permanently give up 1 point of a Physical Attribute’s unaugmented rating, and 1 point of its racial modified limit. Not an Attribute at 1. Taken again, it must be a different Attribute first. | . | Deed | A task fitting the character’s path, group, totem or code, agreed with the GM, or a run that fits. You give up that run’s Karma award. It can be saved, but only for the next initiation. | . | Familiar | Magicians who can summon allies only. Summon an ally spirit that costs at least the initiation’s Karma (with the ordeal). It costs no Magic Point, but if it’s ever banished, freed or destroyed you check for Magic loss. | . | Geas | Take a geas on the new grade’s Magic Point; an adept can put it on the new Power Point. It can never be removed. | . | Meditation | Pass three tests: Charisma against your Strength, Intelligence against your Quickness, Willpower against your Body. Each takes grade × 4 days, divided by its successes. Fail one and the cycle starts again. +2 to all three on a Squatter or Street lifestyle, unless you’re in the wilderness with Wilderness Survival 4+. | . | Oath | Swear to obey a magical group’s rules. For group members only, and only the first oath counts. | . | Thesis | Write or make a formula of all your magical knowledge, as a spell formula of rating 6, 30 days base time. Anyone with a copy has a material link to you, and if every copy is destroyed you lose a Magic Point. | .

125.title: Magical groups  (MitS p.61–65)
125.content: Orders, covens, lodges and circles. What makes one magical is a magical link, its connection to a spirit avatar. Initiating through a group is cheaper, but members live by its rules. | Kinds (MitS p.62): initiatory (magical study first), dedicated (a religious or moral cause) and conspiratorial (power and wealth, often secret and controlling). | Joining costs 3 Karma and the first month’s dues, which other members can pay for you. The group then checks that your “vibes” fit its link (MitS p.65). | Founding one needs two or more Awakened, each paying the 3 Karma. Once a month they roll to establish a link, against TN 12 with modifiers; extra dice cost 3 Karma each (MitS p.65). | Leaving a group you swore an oath to means a check for Magic loss (MitS p.62). | . Strictures (MitS p.62–63) . A group’s rules, tied to its magic. Most have three or four that bind each member: . Attendance · Belief · Deed · Exclusive Membership · Exclusive Ritual · Fraternity · Geas · Obedience · Sacrifice (−1 to every Karma award) · Secrecy . Group strictures, such as Limited Membership or Oath (every member takes the oath ordeal at their first initiation with the group), can only be broken by the group itself, and doing so costs it its link. Breaking a stricture leaves marks in your aura that fellow members can see. When you next initiate, roll Magic against twice the grade you’re seeking, needing at least one success per stricture broken. Pass and the slate is wiped clean. Fail and the group must expel you, or lose its link (MitS p.62).

126.title: Metamagic  (MitS p.69–79)
126.content: | Technique | Page | What it does | . | Anchoring | p.70 | Store a live spell in an anchoring focus, set off by a trigger. | . | Centering | p.72 | Use a creative skill to add successes, resist Drain, or cancel penalties. Below. | . | Cleansing | p.74 | Clear temporary background count, once its cause is gone. | . | Divining | p.74 | Read omens for insight into future events. | . | Invoking | p.75 | Summon great form spirits. | . | Masking | p.76 | Disguise your aura, and see through others’ disguises. | . | Possessing | p.76 | Your astral form enters and controls a living being. | . | Quickening | p.77 | Make a sustained spell permanent without a sustaining focus. | . | Reflecting | p.78 | Spell defense that can turn a spell back on its caster. | . | Shielding | p.79 | A stronger form of spell defense. | . Learning a technique (MitS p.69–70) . One technique per grade, and only one you can use: conjurers and adepts can’t learn Quickening or Shielding, which need Sorcery. Adepts can learn only Centering, Divining and Masking. There are three ways to learn: . | From | The test | Time and price | . | Another initiate of equal or higher grade who knows it | Magic, TN 8 − the teacher’s grade | 14 days ÷ successes. Free within a group; otherwise usually grade × 1,000¥ a day. | . | An astral quest | The quest, rated by the number of techniques you already know (TN at least 2) | Days equal to the quest rating. | . | A free spirit | As from an initiate, with Spirit Energy for grade | Karma, at least its Spirit Energy. Invoking costs double. | . Fail the test and you can try that technique again only at your next grade, on top of that grade’s technique. A third failure, or a roll of all 1s, means you can never learn it. Centering (MitS p.72–74) . Centering uses two skills: Centering, an Active Magical Skill linked to Willpower, and a creative skill such as singing, dancing, an instrument, an arcane language or meditation. Centering can never be higher than the creative skill, and the creative skill can’t come from a chip. Centering is a Free Action in the same phase as the magic it helps, rolled first, and you get only one of its benefits per phase: . | For success: same TN as the magical test. Every 2 successes add a success, but only if the magical test scores at least one. A magician has to be astrally perceiving to do this. | Against Drain: TN = the Drain Power. Every 2 successes count as one Drain Resistance success, if the Drain test scores at least one. | Against penalties: TN = the magical test’s full TN minus your grade. Every 2 successes cancel 1 point of modifiers, never the base TN. | . Adept centering (MitS p.73–74). An adept who learns Centering applies it to Athletics and Stealth. Each later grade can add one more skill area instead of another technique: Build and Repair, Melee Combat, Ranged Combat, Knowledge, Language, Social, Technical, Vehicle, or a Special Skill area. Adepts don’t need astral perception to center for success, and can center against the Drain of their powers, such as Attribute Boost. The book’s example (MitS p.73): Beaumains, a Grade 4 initiate, casts Powerbolt at a target with Body 4, partial cover (+2), poor light (+2), and his own Light Stun (+1): TN 9. He centers on his synthesizer against 9 − 4 = TN 5 and gets 2 successes, cancelling 1 point. He casts at TN 8.

127.title: Geasa  (MitS p.30–33)
127.content: When a character loses a point of Magic, they can take a geas, a restriction on how they use magic, to keep working as if they still had it. A magician with Magic 6 who loses a point is at 5, but with a geas casts as if they had 6. | Decide when the point is lost. Turn the geas down then and you can’t take one for that point later. | At most unaugmented Willpower geasa. At Magic 0 nothing helps: the character is mundane. | A geas only offsets lost points; it never adds Magic. | Break any one and you lose all the points your geasa cover, and take +1 to every Magical Skill test per geas you have, while it stays broken. Astral combat and assensing aren’t affected. | Initiation can shed one geas per grade, instead of gaining Magic. | . Standard geasa (MitS p.32): Condition (unwounded, astrally perceiving…), Domain (the city, the forest…), Exclusive (adepts only: the power can’t be used alongside other magic), Fasting, Gesture, Incantation, Shaman’s (only spells and spirits with a totem advantage), Talisman, and Time (day or night, or a season). The book’s example (MitS p.33): Rikki Ratboy, Magic 6, loses a point to a bad wound and takes the gesture geas, then another to cyberware and takes domain (the city). Shot in a park with a broken arm, he’s broken both. He works at Magic 4, with +2 to all magical tests, until he’s out of the park and his arm is fixed.
