129.title: Karma
129.content: How Karma is earned, how it splits into Good Karma and the Karma Pool, what each one buys, and how the Karma Pool refreshes. From the core rulebook, (SR3 p.242–248), with the magical purchases from the Magic chapter (SR3 p.168, p.180–181, p.190). | Two kinds of Karma (SR3 p.242) | Earning Karma (SR3 p.242, p.244) | Spending Good Karma . | Attributes (SR3 p.244) | Skills (SR3 p.244–245) | Specializations (SR3 p.84, p.245) | Magic (SR3 p.168, p.180–181, p.190) | . | Using the Karma Pool (SR3 p.246) . | Refreshing the pool (SR3 p.104, p.246) | . | Doing it in The 2nd Chumming (Foundry) | .

130.title: Two kinds of Karma  (SR3 p.242)
130.content: Karma is awarded at the end of an adventure, not necessarily after each session. Once awarded it splits in two: . | Good Karma is spent over time to improve the character: Attributes, skills, spells, foci. | Karma Pool is spent during play to get out of trouble: re-rolls, extra dice, avoiding a disaster. | . Every point awarded goes to Good Karma except every twentieth point, which goes to the Karma Pool instead. Humans add every tenth point to their Karma Pool. Every character starts with a Karma Pool of 1 (SR3 p.244). Track Good Karma, Karma Pool and Total Karma (everything ever awarded) separately (SR3 p.242). Worked example, a human (SR3 p.242, p.244): Brynn starts with Karma Pool 1. She is awarded 12 Karma. The tenth point goes to her Pool, which is now 2, and the other 11 are Good Karma. She later earns 9 more, for a Total of 21. The twentieth point goes to her Pool, which is now 3, and the other 8 to Good Karma: 11 + 8 = 19. Worked example, an elf (SR3 p.244): Shetani has a Total Karma of 62. Every twentieth point went to the Pool: 20, 40 and 60 are three points, plus the 1 he started with, so his Pool is 4. The other 59 went to Good Karma, of which he has spent 49, leaving 10.

131.title: Earning Karma  (SR3 p.242, p.244)
131.content: Each surviving member of the team gets Karma for staying alive, for succeeding at the mission and for how dangerous it was. On top of that the gamemaster gives individual awards: . | For | Award (SR3 p.244) | . | Good roleplaying (mostly stayed in character) | 1; excellent roleplaying 2 | . | Guts — brave, effective fighting (not stupidly brave) | 1; particularly heroic 2 | . | Smarts — a clever plan, a solved clue, a good scam, knowing when to run | at least 1 | . | Motivation — driving the story forward | 1 | . | Right place, right time — the vital skill, not known in advance to be needed | 1 | . | Surprise — a strategy that foils the gamemaster’s plans | 1 | . | Humour and drama, in character | 1 | . An amazing run might earn one character 10 or 12 Karma. More than 12 for a single adventure is “highly unlikely” (SR3 p.244). Good dice rolls alone earn nothing.

132.title: Spending Good Karma
132.content: Good Karma is spent between adventures (SR3 p.244). The gamemaster can also require training time, a teacher, or a test to learn or improve something (SR3 p.245). Attributes (SR3 p.244) . Raising a Physical or Mental Attribute by 1 costs 2 × the new rating, using the natural, unaugmented rating. Above the Racial Modified Limit, up to the Attribute Maximum (the limit × 1.5), it costs 3 × the new rating. Strength 5 → 6 costs 12; an elf’s Strength 6 → 7, over her limit of 6, costs 21. Good Karma can’t raise Essence or Magic, even if they were reduced. Reaction isn’t raised directly: raise Quickness and Intelligence instead. Skills (SR3 p.244–245) . A new skill costs 1 at rating 1, whatever its kind. After that, multiply the number on the table by the new rating and round down. The multiplier depends on the skill’s linked Attribute (natural rating) at the time you buy. Skill Improvement Cost Table (SR3 p.245) . | New rating is… | Active Skill | Knowledge / Language Skill | . | Less than or equal to the Attribute | 1.5 | 1 | . | Less than or equal to 2 × the Attribute | 2 | 1.5 | . | More than 2 × the Attribute | 2.5 | 2 | . | New specialization rating is… | Active | Knowledge / Language | . | Less than or equal to the Attribute | .5 | .5 | . | Less than or equal to 2 × the Attribute | 1 | 1 | . | More than 2 × the Attribute | 1.5 | 1.5 | . Worked example (SR3 p.245): Iris has Pistols 3 and Quickness 4. Pistols 4 costs 4 × 1.5 = 6. Pistols 5 is over her Quickness, so it costs 5 × 2 = 10. Specializations (SR3 p.84, p.245) . | A new specialization is bought one point above the base skill, as if it were already at the base skill’s rating and being raised. The base skill isn’t reduced. | You can have as many specializations of a skill as its linked Attribute’s rating. | A specialization can’t be more than twice its base skill (a base skill of 1 may have a specialization of 3). Raise the base skill first. | Specializations don’t rise when the base skill does; each is raised separately. | . Worked example (SR3 p.245): Brick has Stealth 5 and Quickness 6. A new Sneaking specialization starts at 6: 6 × .5 = 3. Raising it to 7, over his Quickness, would cost 7 × 1 = 7. There are no refunds if a later Attribute increase would have made a purchase cheaper (SR3 p.245). Magic (SR3 p.168, p.180–181, p.190) . | Purchase | Good Karma | . | An adept’s extra Power Point, during play (SR3 p.168) | 20 each | . | Learning a spell (SR3 p.180) | the desired Force (a failed attempt costs no Karma) | . | …with a limit (fetish, exclusive) taken on the cost (SR3 p.180) | the Force minus the limit’s modifier | . | Bonding a focus (SR3 p.190) | from the table below | . Focus Bonding Table (SR3 p.190) . | Item | Karma cost | . | Expendable Spell Focus | 0 | . | Specific Spell Focus | 1 × Force | . | Spell Category Focus | 3 × Force | . | Spirit Focus | 2 × Force | . | Power Focus | 5 × Force | . | Sustaining Focus | 1 × Force | . | Weapon Focus | (3 + Weapon Reach) × Force | . Worked example (SR3 p.181): learning Fireball at Force 8 with a −2 limit taken on the cost costs 8 − 2 = 6 Karma. Initiation, quickening, allies and the rest of Magic in the Shadows also cost Good Karma; they aren’t covered here yet.

133.title: Using the Karma Pool  (SR3 p.246)
133.content: The Karma Pool is spent during play. Some uses spend points, which come back when the pool refreshes. Others burn them, which removes them permanently: “burned Karma Pool dice do not refresh” (SR3 p.246). | Use (SR3 p.246) | Cost | Spent or burned | . | Re-roll failures — re-roll every die in a test that failed | 1 the first time; 2 more for a second re-roll of the same test, 3 more for a third… | spent | . | Avoid a disaster — every die came up 1 (Rule of One, SR3 p.38) | 1: the disaster becomes a simple failure | spent | . | Open Test re-roll | 1 for one die, 2 more for a second (3 in all), 3 more for a third (6)… | spent | . | Buy additional dice — up to the skill, Attribute or rating dice you’re using, not counting dice from other pools | 1 for one die, 2 more for a second, 3 more for a third… | spent | . | Buy successes — only if the test already scored at least one | 1 per success | burned | . | Extended actions — Karma Pool committed when a long task begins (SR3 p.246, 248; gamemaster’s option) | as committed; the pool doesn’t refresh until the task is done | spent | . | The Hooper-Nelson rule — lower a spectacularly difficult target number (SR3 p.248; gamemaster’s option) | 1 per point of TN; recommended only at TN 12 or more, and never below 8 | burned | . A few limits worth knowing: . | A success can’t be re-rolled. Only the failed dice go again. | An “oops” roll can’t be re-rolled. On a Rule of One, the only use is avoiding the disaster. | Each re-roll of the same test costs more. Re-rolling twice costs 1 + 2 = 3 in all; three times, 6. | . Worked example (SR3 p.246): Dodger rolls Electronics B/R 5 against TN 8 and gets one success. He needs four, so he spends 1 Karma Pool to re-roll the four failed dice. Refreshing the pool (SR3 p.104, p.246) . The Karma Pool doesn’t refresh every Combat Turn like other dice pools. It refreshes when the gamemaster says so, roughly once per scene of the story: every 24 hours of game time, or a matter of hours or days (SR3 p.104, p.246). In most games it refreshes at the start of each session. The gamemaster can bend this: characters on the run may not get to refresh, a breather between encounters may refresh some or all of it, and one character can refresh faster than another. A character near death might not refresh until healed, while one pulling off heroic stunts might refresh in short order (SR3 p.246). Only what was spent comes back. Burned points are gone.

134.title: Doing it in The 2nd Chumming (Foundry)
134.content: The system tracks everything above and charges it when you use it, but nothing is refused: the gamemaster can edit any number. On the sheet . | Bio → Resources holds Good Karma and Total Karma, with Spend Karma… for players and Award Karma… for the gamemaster. Awards split themselves: the tenth or twentieth point goes to the Pool. | Attributes → Derived Pools shows the Karma Pool as left / size. Spending lowers “left”; burning lowers the size. | The 📒 Ledger on the Bio tab records every change, with the reason: “Pool spent” for spends, “Karma Pool” for burns. | . Spend Karma… lists every purchase you can afford, priced from the tables above: Attributes (it says when you’re over the Racial Modified Limit), skills, new skills, specializations (an amber warning past twice the base skill), and under Magic an adept’s Power Point, learning a spell (you choose the Force and any limit) and bonding a focus. The gamemaster can ↺ undo any purchase from its ledger line: the Karma comes back and the purchase is reversed, recorded as a new line. On a roll, every roll dialog has a 🍀 row: . | Buy extra dice: the cost (1, 3, 6…) is spent as the roll is made. | Hold the roll for Karma: the finished dice wait on a 🍀 card before anything happens. From there you can re-roll the failures, avoid a disaster, or buy successes, then press ✔ Done. Only you (and the gamemaster) can press those buttons. | Hooper-Nelson: burn points to lower the TN, never below 8. It warns under TN 12, because it’s the gamemaster’s option. | . Refreshing is the gamemaster’s: 🍀 Refresh on a character’s sheet, or 🍀 Refresh Karma Pools among the GM tools (Rollable Tables tab) for the whole party. Reset All Pools doesn’t touch the Karma Pool. 136.title: How they got here  (SR3 p.31–35)
136.content: . | 2033: Damien Knight’s “Nanosecond Buyout”. A burst of computer-driven trades gave Knight 22% of Ares. He and CEO Leonard Aurelius loathed each other from the start (SR3 p.31). | 2034: Richard Villiers bought a failed tech company cheaply after its founders died, then used its “lost” research to buy his way into Fuchi (SR3 p.31). | 2037: Lofwyr revealed that he owned 63% of the company behind BMW, and renamed it Saeder-Krupp (SR3 p.31). | 2041–42: Yamatetsu forced its way onto the Corporate Court, turning the Big Seven into the Big Eight (SR3 p.31). | 2048: Operation Reciprocity. The corps struck Aztechnology jointly after Aztlan nationalised them (SR3 p.31). | 2058–59: The corp war begins. Miles Lanier left Fuchi for Renraku’s board, Fuchi’s three factions turned on each other, and Villiers formed Novatech to take his share out. Yamatetsu’s chairman died in 2059 and left his shares to his ork son; rather than depose him, Yamatetsu moved its headquarters to Vladivostok. Ares Macrotechnology (NS p.89–90) . The military-industrial giant, led mostly by ex-military execs. In Seattle it avoids a costly war with Federated-Boeing and works with it instead, as a sub-contractor and ally. Its security subsidiary Knight Errant guards its buildings, and Ares Arms tests prototypes on KE. Its feud with Cross is personal: Leonard Aurelius, Knight’s old rival, sold his Ares stock and backed Cross, and his son now runs Cross’s Seattle division (NS p.91). Aztechnology (NS p.81, p.90) . Banned from California and Tir Tairngire, so Seattle is where it pulls the strings on its business there, through shells and holding companies. At least one battalion of Aztlan troops is stationed in Seattle. Runners describe a layered magical defence of watcher spirits and then elementals, and rumours of blood magic in the sub-basements. Its Matrix host has a link to the Tenochtitlán home office. It is Aztlan’s corp in all but name, and relations between Aztlan and Seattle are “cool but cordial” (NS p.81). Cross Applied Technologies (SR3 p.35; NS p.90–91) . A second-tier corp from Quebec pushing into the UCAS market, and paying for it: the Big Eight want no more newcomers, and Lucien Cross survived three assassination attempts in 2058 alone (SR3 p.35). Its black-ops division is the Seraphim. Runners say Cross prefers to take intruders alive, and its Matrix ice traces you so it can collect a favour later. Its people have been seen visiting the Draco Foundation. The Draco Foundation . Set up by Dunkelzahn’s will to administer his bequests, with Nadja Daviar as chair (SR3 p.34). In Seattle it is run by Sassinian, a sasquatch. The Council of Princes refused it an office in the Tir, so the Seattle office covers the Tir as well. New Seattle calls it “a big-big-big employer of shadowrunners”: it has plenty of money and a will to carry out (NS p.91–92). It also sits on the UCC (NS p.83). Fuchi Industrial Electronics (SR3 p.34–35) . A Big Eight computer giant tearing itself apart. Fuchi has three internal factions, and the corp war with Renraku has made their feud worse. In mid-2059 Fuchi accused Renraku of stealing its secrets through Miles Lanier, its former security chief; the charges were dropped. Richard Villiers, expecting the other factions to force him out, has formed Novatech and is quietly buying his Fuchi North America holdings into it. He has offered Lanier the job of Novatech’s head of security. Every faction, and every rival, wants to know what happens to Fuchi next, which means steady work for runners. Mitsuhama Computer Technologies (NS p.92–93) . It aims for the top spot in computing while Fuchi and Renraku fight. Runners credit it with the “zero-zone”: zero penetration, zero survival. That means concealed autoguns, lethal gas, barghest guard dogs, bound elementals, and black ice that kills. Its wage mages are Unit 13, which is mostly human, with no shamans. Its Johnsons want the job done exactly as planned. For its “special problems” it can call on the Seattle yakuza. Renraku Computer Systems (SR3 p.34–35) . Fuchi’s great rival, and lately the winner: months after Miles Lanier joined its board in 2058, Renraku began producing remarkable technological advances. Fuchi’s espionage charges in mid-2059 were dropped, but Lanier left Renraku and sold his stock to the Zurich-Orbital bank. In Seattle, Renraku is the Arcology: a self-contained corporate city that houses nearly 100,000 people (NS p.30). Saeder-Krupp (SR3 p.31; NS p.94–95) . Owned by the great dragon Lofwyr, and called the world’s largest megacorp. Officially it has no presence in Seattle. Unofficially it has subsidiaries, small offices, and watchers posted by Lofwyr. “The biggest business Saeder-Krupp does in Seattle is shadow business,” and nobody can predict what it will want. Shiawase (NS p.76, p.95–96) . The Shiawase decision that created extraterritoriality is named after this corp (SR3 p.22). Shiawase Atomics maintains Seattle’s power grid, and wants Gaeatronics’s generating contract (NS p.76). Its spy network often knows a run is coming. Its defences use net-guns and knockout gas, and its ice is mostly trace, because it wants prisoners to interrogate. Wuxing (SR3 p.35; NS p.81, p.96) . A small family corp until Dunkelzahn’s money raised it to the top. In 2059 Wuxing took the Corporate Court seat left empty when Fuchi’s representative died (SR3 p.35). It drives the Pacific Prosperity Group, a trade bloc against Japanese economic dominance. That makes it an enemy of the Japanese corps, and a rival of Federated-Boeing, which is also in the PPG. Runners expect the Triads to work on its behalf. Yamatetsu (SR3 p.35; NS p.96) . When chairman Tadamako Shibanokuji died in 2059, his shares went to his son Yuri, an ork. Pressed to depose him, Yamatetsu instead moved its headquarters to Vladivostok (SR3 p.35). It now sells itself as the meta-friendly, “Awakened” corp, and its traditionalist staff are fighting that change. It has no friends among the other Japanese corps (NS p.96).

145.title: What an adept is  (SR3 p.55, p.168)
145.content: Adepts follow the somatic way. They don’t cast spells or conjure spirits, and they have no access to astral space unless they buy the Astral Perception power. They can never astrally project. What they get instead are powers, magical abilities that become a natural part of the adept through training (SR3 p.55, p.168). An adept can still use Sorcery in astral combat (SR3 p.168). | At character creation an adept takes Magic at Priority B, the same priority as an aspected magician; a full magician needs Priority A (SR3 p.54). | Adepts get no Spell Points. They can buy weapon foci with nuyen, but can’t bond one until they have the Karma (SR3 p.55, p.60). | .

146.title: Power Points  (SR3 p.55, p.168)
146.content: . | An adept starts with Power Points equal to their Magic Attribute, 6 in most cases. At character creation they can’t buy or sell extra Power Points (SR3 p.55). | Each power costs Power Points. Once spent they’re gone, and the choice of powers is permanent (SR3 p.168). | No power can have more levels than the adept’s Magic. An adept with Magic 4 has at most 4 points of powers, and none of more than four levels (SR3 p.168). | During play, an adept can buy more Power Points at 20 Good Karma each (SR3 p.168). See Karma. | . Losing Magic (SR3 p.160, p.168) . Every full point of Essence lost, or fraction of one, costs a point of Magic: an adept with Essence 5.8 and Magic 5 loses another point of Magic when Essence drops below 5. Deadly wounds, bad medical care, drug abuse and disruption in astral combat can also call for a Magic Loss check: roll 2D6, and if the total is less than or equal to your Magic, it drops by one. A roll of 2 always costs the point (SR3 p.160). An adept who loses a point of Magic loses a point’s worth of powers. The player chooses which (SR3 p.168). At Magic 0 the character burns out and is mundane forever (SR3 p.160).

The base range TNs are Short 4, Medium 5, Long 6 and Extreme 9 (SR3 p.110), so a long-range arrow is TN 10 − 6 = 4. 150.title: Doing it in The 2nd Chumming (Foundry)
150.content: Making a character an adept . On the Magic tab, set the magic type to Adept. The tab then shows an Adept Powers list with Power Points: used / total, where the total is Magic plus any Power Points bought with Karma. Add powers by dragging them from the compendiums (Shadowrun 3rd, Magic in the Shadows and State of the Art 2064 under Adept Powers), or with + Add Power. Give a levelled power its level on the row. The system warns, and never refuses: . | Power Points over the total turn the count red. | A power with more levels than Magic is listed under Above Magic (SR3 p.168). | Improved Reflexes stacked with wired reflexes or a spell gets a warning, and the sheet applies the better package only (SR3 p.169). | Powers the system can describe but not resolve are listed as Applied by the GM, with what each one does. | . What the system does with each power . | Power | Where it shows up | . | Improved Physical Attribute | Added to the Attribute (per level). | . | Improved Reflexes | Reaction and Initiative dice. | . | Improved Ability | Extra dice on the skill, capped at the lesser of the skill and Magic. 154.content: Seattle is a UCAS city surrounded by NAN territory. Since 2042 it has been allowed to send its own envoys abroad (NS p.80). 171.title: Part 1: the rules
171.content: Vehicle Attributes (SR3 p.130–133) . Vehicles have their own Attribute Ratings, the way characters have Attributes. The ones that come up at the table: . | Handling — how easy the vehicle is to control. Confusingly, a higher Handling is worse: it’s the base target number for Driving Tests. | Speed and Acceleration — top safe speed (meters per Combat Turn) and how fast that speed can change on a successful Driving Test. Pushing past 1.5× Speed, or braking too hard, gets punished elsewhere in these rules. | Body and Armor — how much punishment the vehicle takes before it won’t take any more, and how much of an incoming hit’s Power gets stopped outright or reduced. Vehicle armor is hardened: it blocks a hit completely if that hit’s Power (after the mass reduction below) doesn’t clear the rating. | Signature — the target number sensors and missiles need to lock the vehicle; ordinary gunfire aimed by eye ignores it. | Autonav — the onboard autopilot’s rating. It helps outside combat and gets in the way during it (see the vehicle-combat actions below). | Pilot — a drone’s own decision-making rating, used in place of a skill when nobody is driving it. | Sensor — the vehicle’s Perception dice, and a small boost to Gunnery. | A handful of others (Cargo Factor, Load, Seating, Entry Points) are bookkeeping rather than dice. | . Riggers, jacking in, and Control Pool (SR3 p.44, p.130, p.140, p.301) . A rigger carries a Vehicle Control Rig (VCR), cyberware that lets them drive a suitably wired vehicle through a neural link instead of a wheel or yoke. Jacked in this way, a rigger gets several things an ordinary driver doesn’t: . | A better Initiative. Each VCR level is worth +2 Reaction and one extra Initiative die while rigging (SR3 p.301). This is a replacement, not a stack: wired reflexes, boosted reflexes, and magical or adept increases to Reaction or Initiative do not apply for a rigger determining Initiative this way (SR3 p.140). | A Control Pool. This works like Combat Pool or Spell Pool but is spent only on tests to control the rigged vehicle: driving, dodging incoming fire, and resisting collision damage. Its size is simply the rigger’s own Reaction plus twice their VCR level — nothing else adds to it — and any single test can only draw as many Control Pool dice as it has base skill dice (SR3 p.44). No VCR means no Control Pool at all, even for a rigger driving a vehicle they aren’t currently jacked into. | An easier default. A VCR lets its user default to Reaction for any Vehicle Skill test at only +2 to the target number, instead of the usual +4 for defaulting to an unrelated attribute (SR3 p.301). | Riggers can alternatively jack into a remote control deck to run drones from a distance instead of riding in them. Left with no driver at all, a drone falls back on its own Pilot Rating in place of a skill. | . The Driving Test (SR3 p.134) . Ordinary vehicle handling — a difficult maneuver, not vehicle combat — is a Complex Action: the appropriate Vehicle Skill against a base target number equal to the vehicle’s Handling. An active autonav adds dice equal to its own rating outside combat; a jacked-in rigger can add Control Pool dice (up to their skill rating) instead of the autonav bonus, on top of reducing the target number by their VCR level. Driving without rigging (SR3 p.130, p.134) . Most drivers at the table aren’t riggers at all — a street samurai taking the wheel, a face on a motorcycle. Nothing above changes for them except that the rigger-only pieces simply don’t apply: . | They still make an ordinary Driving Test — Vehicle Skill against the vehicle’s Handling — and still get an active autonav’s dice outside combat. They never have a Control Pool to add on top, because that pool only exists for someone jacked into a VCR. | With no Vehicle Skill at all, they use the same Default Table everyone else defaults from: typically falling back on Reaction at the ordinary +4 target-number penalty for defaulting to an unrelated attribute. The VCR’s +2 discount above is specific to a rigger with that cyberware and doesn’t extend to anyone else. | Driving through a datajack without a VCR — or a VCR-equipped rigger driving a vehicle that isn’t itself wired for rigger control — gets a small −1 break on the target number (the datajack row on the table above), but still earns no Control Pool. | Their Initiative is rolled the ordinary way for their character, with none of a rigger’s VCR bonus, whether or not they happen to be driving that turn. | Crash Tests, ramming, and the driver/passenger collision-damage rules below apply to them exactly the same as to a rigger. The only things rigging adds there are Control Pool dice to soften the hit and the separate p.145 rigger-feedback damage — neither of which touches someone driving by hand. | . Vehicle combat and the Maneuver Score (SR3 p.138–144) . Once a chase or a fight turns into an actual vehicle-combat scene, the book layers on a Maneuver Score: a number rebuilt every Combat Turn from the vehicle’s type (nimble vehicles like motorcycles score well, lumbering ones like heavy trucks score poorly), the terrain, roughly how fast the vehicle is going, and Driver Points — an Open Test (every 6 is rerolled and added, as many times as it keeps coming up) using the Vehicle Skill, plus any Control Pool dice the rigger allocates for it. Each driver then picks one Complex Action per turn from a short list, each with its own modifier table: . | Accelerating or braking — a Driving Test against Handling; success changes speed by Acceleration times the successes rolled. | Positioning — banks successes as a bonus to next turn’s Maneuver Score, buying a better tactical spot. | Ramming — see below. | Hiding — breaking contact with a pursuer, whose successes make it harder for the follower to relocate the hider next turn. | Relocating — the pursuer’s answer to a vehicle that just hid. | Or simply doing something that isn’t driving — firing a personal weapon, working the electronics, and so on — as an ordinary action instead. | . A successful Hiding Test also earns an Escape Bonus equal to its successes, added to Driver Points each turn until the pursuer relocates the hider (a Relocating Test — a Sensor or Perception Test against the hider’s Signature, made harder by the hider’s own Hiding successes and by a similar set of Maneuver Score and terrain modifiers, in reverse). Vehicle armor is hardened: a hit whose Power (after the vehicle-mass halving below) doesn’t exceed the Armor Rating does nothing at all; otherwise Armor reduces Power like ordinary armor. Shooting a vehicle, and shooting from one (SR3 p.149) . A vehicle’s size works in its favour against gunfire: an attack aimed at the vehicle itself has its Power halved and its Damage Level dropped a step before the vehicle’s own Armor is applied, and a weapon too weak to do more than Light damage can’t scratch a vehicle at all without special ammunition. Anti-vehicle ammunition skips that halving, and only loses half the Armor Rating rather than the whole thing. The vehicle resists with Body dice plus any Control Pool a jacked-in rigger can add (capped at their skill), against the reduced Power. A rigger may dodge instead of soaking, spending Control Pool against Handling in place of Combat Pool. Shooting passengers inside the vehicle is harder than shooting the vehicle itself: the shot loses Power equal to whichever of the vehicle’s Armor or Body is higher, and if that wipes the Power out entirely nobody inside can be hurt by it. Passengers only get half their usual Combat Pool for Dodge or resistance, and a rigger who is jacked in — their attention is in the vehicle, not their own body — can’t dodge at all and takes a target-number penalty on their own resistance roll. Vehicle damage, Crash Tests, and ramming (SR3 p.145–148) . Vehicles only track physical damage, staged Light through Destroyed the same way a character stages Light through Deadly, each level adding its own target-number penalty, Initiative penalty and Speed reduction. Vehicle Damage Modifiers Table (SR3 p.147) . | Damage Level | Target number modifier | Initiative penalty | Speed reduction | . | Light | +1 | −1 | none | . | Moderate | +2 | −2 | 25% | . | Serious | +3 | −3 | 50% | . A vehicle that reaches Destroyed is no longer operable. (SR3 p.149) . The Power of a crash or a ram is the relevant speed, in meters per Combat Turn, divided by ten and rounded up. Impact Damage Levels Table (SR3 p.147) . | Vehicle speed (m/turn) | Damage Level | . | 1–20 | Light | . | 21–60 | Moderate | . | 61–200 | Serious | . | 201+ | Destroyed | . A Crash Test — a Driving Test against Handling — comes up whenever a vehicle takes Serious damage in one hit, gets rammed and hurt by it, bottoms out its Condition Monitor, or brakes far harder than its Acceleration allows. Both the autonav bonus and Control Pool dice can help here. Failing it means the vehicle stops dead and has to resist the impact on top of whatever caused the crash in the first place. Crash Test Modifiers Table (SR3 p.148) . | Condition | Modifier | . | Driver wounded | + the wound’s damage modifier | . | Vehicle already damaged | + the vehicle’s own damage modifier | . | Terrain: open / normal / restricted / tight | −1 / 0 / +2 / +4 | . | Speed less than driver’s Reaction × 20 | 0 | . | Speed less than Reaction × 30 | +1 | . | Speed less than Reaction × 40 | +2 | . | Speed more than Reaction × 40 | +4 | . Ramming: the ramming vehicle rolls a Ramming Test (Driving Skill against Handling, modified by the table above). On a success, both vehicles resist a collision at a Power equal to their speed difference ÷ 10, rounded up, at the Damage Level the Impact table gives that speed difference. The rammer’s own successes on the Ramming Test reduce the Power of the collision — for the rammer’s own resistance roll only — by their vehicle’s Body Rating times those successes, floored so the resulting target number never drops below 2. The target’s Damage Code is untouched by that reduction. Either side that ends up taking damage from the collision then owes its own Crash Test. Everyone aboard shares the hit. Whenever the vehicle takes damage — crash, ram, or gunfire — the driver and every passenger resist the same Power the vehicle faced, but at whatever Level the vehicle actually ended up taking after its own soak, not the raw Level before that. A seat belt knocks that Level down one further step, and only impact armor (never Ballistic) counts against it. A jacked-in rigger takes a second, separate hit. Beyond what their body feels as a passenger, the neural feedback of a Serious hit to “their” vehicle forces a Willpower-resisted Physical Damage Resistance Test — no Combat or Control Pool allowed — against a fixed 6M; if the vehicle is destroyed outright, that becomes 6S (SR3 p.145). Dump shock for a rigger (SR3 p.156) . Getting forcibly kicked out of a rigged connection hits a rigger harder than the equivalent shock hits a decker, because the VCR link runs deeper into the nervous system. There are two distinct triggers, and vehicle destruction is not one of them — that case is the fixed 6S Physical hit above, from p.145: . | Dumped from a remote-control network: resist a Stun Damage Resistance Test with Willpower, at a Power equal to the deck’s own Rating + 4. On top of that, the rigger suffers ten Combat Turns of disorientation, adding +2 to every Success Test they make during that window. | Involuntarily jacked out of a vehicle, other than by its destruction (forced out some other way, mid-scene): resist a flat 5S Stun instead, plus the same ten turns of disorientation. | . The disorientation can be shortened: a Willpower Test against target number 4, then divide 30 by the successes (round up) for the number of seconds disoriented, then divide that by 3 (round up) for how many Combat Turns the effect actually lasts. Autonav and Pilot for drones (SR3 p.132–133, p.157) . A driverless drone substitutes its own Pilot Rating for whatever skill or attribute the test would otherwise use. Giving it anything more specific than a standing order is a Drone Comprehension test: the Pilot Rating rolled against a target number the GM sets by how complicated the instruction is — one success gets it followed, more successes buy the drone some leeway in how it’s carried out (SR3 p.157). Electronic warfare against a rigger or their drones — jamming, signal degradation, intrusion and the rest — is a large enough topic that it gets summarised on the Decking page rather than repeated here; see Decking and, for what this system actually implements, Part 2 below.

172.title: Part 2: doing it in The 2nd Chumming (Foundry)
172.content: The system never applies vehicle damage automatically, same as everywhere else: it rolls dice, stages damage, and posts a button — the GM clicks the wound boxes. Not everyone behind the wheel is rigging, either — see Driving without rigging, in Foundry below for the ordinary case. Getting a vehicle onto a character’s sheet . A vehicle is its own actor, with its own sheet (Stats / Weapons / Mods / Electronic Warfare / Notes tabs). To give a character a vehicle: . | Drag the vehicle actor onto the character sheet. Dragging a compendium vehicle deploys a working copy and sets that character as its driver; dragging an existing world vehicle links it to that character instead. Both routes run through the GM so the character ends up with owner permission on the new or linked vehicle actor, whether or not a Player has permission to create actors directly. | Or, on the character sheet’s Vehicles tab, click + Add Vehicle, which opens the same dialog with three sources: link an existing world vehicle, create a blank one, or pull one from a compendium. | The Vehicles tab lists every vehicle whose pilot is this character, with its Handling/Speed/Body/Armor/Pilot/Sensor at a glance, a link to open its sheet, and per-vehicle VCR / RCD / Auto mode buttons plus a ✕ to unlink it (the vehicle itself isn’t deleted — it can be added back). | On the vehicle’s own sheet, the Pilot dropdown sets who drives it, and Passengers (add/remove tags in the header) tracks who else is aboard — this is the roster a crash or ram reaches, without needing a Chase Scene open. | . Jacking in: VCR / RCD / Auto . Each vehicle has one of three control modes, toggled from either the vehicle sheet’s header or the character sheet’s Vehicles tab: . | VCR — the pilot is jacked in with a Vehicle Control Rig. The system reads the rigger’s own VCR item (a cyberware item with “VCR” or “vehicle control rig” in its name) for its level, and uses Reaction (base, unaugmented) plus twice that level for both Initiative and Control Pool — wired reflexes and magical Reaction boosts are excluded, matching the book. VCR is exclusive: setting one vehicle to VCR automatically drops any other vehicle that character was VCR-driving to RCD, and turns off VR Matrix modes on the character (VCR and VR can’t both be active). | RCD — remote control deck, the book’s captain’s chair: a rigger with a VCR keeps the VCR Initiative, one without uses their ordinary Reaction and Initiative dice. The drone’s own tests (weapons, Driving and Crash Tests) roll its Pilot Rating, with no pools (SR3 p.154). See Drones. | Auto — nobody is piloting; the vehicle rolls its own Initiative from its Pilot Rating, and clearing this mode also clears the vehicle’s pilot. | . A vehicle in VCR or RCD mode copies its rigger’s Initiative for Combat Turn ordering rather than rolling its own. The book’s VCR-specific default reduction (Reaction at +2 instead of the usual +4, above) isn’t modeled: the Default Table a driver with no Vehicle Skill sees is the same generic one used everywhere else in the system, with no VCR-aware discount. This is tracked in the codebase as TODO 106. Driving without rigging, in Foundry . A character with no VCR item at all — the ordinary case — still uses the same 🚗 Driving Test dialog described just below. The “Using VCR” option in it only shows up once the system finds VCR cyberware on the driver; without one, the pool simply builds as Vehicle Skill plus Autonav, with no Control Pool line at all, since the underlying Control Pool calculation returns zero for anyone without a VCR rating. The vehicle’s control-mode button is normally left on RCD for this case: mechanically, “no VCR bonus” is one path whether the driver is remote-piloting a drone or simply sitting behind the wheel, so the same Reaction-based Initiative and pool math cover both, and the mode buttons are shared between them. Defaulting with no matching Vehicle Skill opens the same Default Table dialog described in the note above — it always offers the ordinary +4-to-an- attribute default, with no special case for a rigger’s +2. Driving Tests and Crash Tests . | 🚗 Driving Test, from the vehicle sheet’s Stats tab (only shown once a pilot is set) or the Rollable Tables sidebar tab (available to everyone, not just the GM), asks for the vehicle and driver, then builds the pool automatically: Vehicle Skill plus Autonav normally, or Vehicle Skill plus Control Pool dice (capped at the skill) once “Using VCR” is selected for a jacked-in rigger. The target number starts at Handling and offers the standard dropdowns — unfamiliar, stressful, size, weather, terrain, combat, datajack, and the VCR reduction. No Vehicle Skill on the driver opens the Default Table dialog instead of refusing the roll. | 💥 Crash, from the same Stats tab menu (or the Vehicle Tools HUD on a token, or the 💥 button offered after a failed Driving Test), gives two ways in: rolling the Crash Test as the driver, so a failure posts the crash automatically, or posting crash damage directly for when the accident has already happened and there’s no test left to make. Either way it ends at the same damage builder: speed (asked in km/h and converted to meters per Combat Turn for the table), a Power and Level that follow the vehicle’s speed until the GM edits them by hand, and a checklist of who’s aboard (seeded from the vehicle’s pilot/passenger roster) to resist afterward. | Ramming and collisions post the same occupant-resistance chain: after the vehicle’s own soak roll, the driver and every passenger get a resist-collision-damage button, which opens a small dialog asking for their Body dice, their impact armor (pre-filled from worn and implanted armor), and whether they were belted in, and shows the resulting Power/Level/target number live before they roll. If the vehicle itself took no damage, the card says so and nobody rolls. | . Dump shock, and rigger damage from a destroyed vehicle . | ⚡ Dump Shock is a button in the character sheet’s Rigger — Electronic Warfare panel (and beside the Matrix tools when in VR). Its dialog asks what the character was dumped from: the Matrix (a decker), a remote-control network, which uses the RC deck Rating from the panel, or a vehicle they were jacked out of. The rigger cases post the book’s Power, (Rating + 4)S or 5S Stun. The resist card rolls Willpower, with no armor. The card also states the ten turns of +2 disorientation and offers the Willpower (4) Test that shortens it; that roll’s result card says how many Combat Turns it lasts. | Rigger damage is offered automatically. When a vehicle a rigger is jacked into (VCR mode) reaches Serious, a card offers the rigger the 6M Physical resistance, and when it is Destroyed, 6S. The roll is Willpower with no Combat or Control Pool and no armor. Nothing is applied: the rigger rolls, and the wound goes on only when someone clicks 🩸 Assign. | . The Chase Scene (combat tracker) . The 🚗 Chase Scene tool, opened from the Rollable Tables sidebar tab (open to every player, not just the GM), implements the book’s vehicle-combat maneuver system rather than standing in for it with something simpler: it tracks each participant’s vehicle type, terrain and speed, computes their Maneuver Score, and offers dedicated action buttons for Accel/Brake, Positioning, Ramming, Hiding and Relocating, each opening a dialog with the relevant modifiers pre-filled and live target-number and pool math. One participant can be flagged Quarry — everyone else’s distance is then tracked relative to it (positive behind, negative ahead), and at the end of each turn the tool updates every pursuer’s distance from the speed difference automatically, reporting who’s closing and who’s falling behind. Driver Points get the same reroll-on-6 handling as every other open-ended roll in the system. Drones and remote control . A vehicle actor typed as a drone works the same way as any other vehicle — Pilot dropdown, VCR/RCD/Auto modes — except its natural state is Auto, running on its own Pilot Rating. 📡 Drone Comprehension (Stats tab, or the Vehicle Tools HUD) rolls Pilot Rating dice, no pool, against a GM-set target number, with any Command-channel electronic-warfare degradation folded in automatically. Zero successes means the drone does nothing useful; one gets the order followed literally; two or more gives it some leeway. Electronic warfare, briefly . Jamming, Flux/Footprint, ECM/ECCM, MIJI attacks and signal degradation on a rigger or their drones live on the vehicle sheet’s Electronic Warfare tab and the ⚡ MIJI Attack / 📶 IVIS Test tools; they aren’t repeated here. Ask the GM what’s actually running at your table, or see Decking for the related Matrix rules.

173.title: Worked example: a ramming attempt
173.content: Dex is jacked into his step-van (Handling 4, Body 8) with Car Skill 5 and a Rating-2 VCR, chasing a patrol car (Handling 4, Body 3) driven by an unrigged cop with Car Skill 4. Dex’s van is doing 96 meters a turn to the patrol car’s 60. For this Combat Turn, assume Dex’s Maneuver Score came out to 42 against the patrol car’s 28 — a gap of more than 10 in Dex’s favor. | Control Pool. Reaction 5 plus twice his VCR level (2) gives Dex a Control Pool of 9 dice, though any one test can only draw up to his 5 Car Skill dice from it. | The Ramming Test. Base target number is his van’s Handling, 4. His Maneuver Score beats the patrol car’s by more than 10 (−4); terrain is normal (0); his VCR knocks off a further 2 × his Rating 2 (−4). Total modifier −8 against a base of 4 gives a target number of −4, floored at the rule’s minimum of 2. He rolls his 5 Car Skill dice (no Control Pool needed at this target number) and gets 3 successes: the ram connects. | Working out the Power. The two vehicles are 36 meters a turn apart in speed; divided by ten and rounded up, that’s a Power of 4, landing as Moderate on the Impact Damage Levels Table (21–60 m/turn). | Dex’s own resistance. Because he was the one ramming, his 3 Ramming successes reduce the Power of the collision for his own resistance test by his Body (8) times those successes — 24 points, which would take Power below zero, so his target number floors at 2. Rolling Body 8 (plus Control Pool if he wanted it, though he doesn’t need it here) against target number 2, his van shrugs the impact off. | The patrol car’s resistance isn’t reduced by anything Dex rolled: it faces the full Moderate hit at Power 4, resisting with its own Body 3 dice (no VCR, so no Control Pool for the cop) against target number . | Say the gamemaster rolls 1 success — not enough to stage a Moderate hit down a level, which needs 2 — so the car takes the Moderate wound outright, and because it took damage from a ram, its driver now owes a Crash Test. | . | The cop. Riding in the car that just got hit, the driver resists the same Power at the same Level the car ended up taking — Moderate at Power 4 — reduced further by whatever impact armor he’s wearing and by a seat belt if he has one buckled. | .

181.title: What a SIN is  (SR3 p.238)
181.content: . | The UCAS introduced SINs in 2036, requiring every citizen to register. 182.title: Life with a SIN  (SR3 p.238–239)
182.content: You need a SIN to get a legal job, open a bank account, own property, go to school, rent an apartment, set up utilities, and travel legally, which includes buying a bus ticket. Your credstick carries your ID, licenses and permits, and can hold your fingerprints, palmprints and retinal prints. The cost is a data trail. Every legal purchase leaves credit records and inventory, and possibly video footage, and stores that realize they sold to shadowrunners will hand those records to the police. (SR3 p.273) .

183.title: Life without one  (SR3 p.238)
183.content: . | You officially don’t exist, which makes you hard to trace. | If you’re arrested, you may be abused, locked away or “disappeared”, with no data trail to prove you existed. More often you’re issued a criminal SIN, which is yours for life and is stored in police databases with your photograph, fingerprints and perhaps more. | Legal work, housing and travel are all closed to you. | . Players decide at character creation whether their character has a SIN. (SR3 p.238) .

185.title: Fake IDs: forging credsticks  (SR3 p.239)
185.content: Faking an identity means inserting a believable credit history into databases all over the world. Only well-connected forgery outfits, often based in data havens, can do it. 197.title: Step 1: Preparation  (SR3 p.178, p.181, p.191)
197.content: Decide all of these before rolling. | The spell and its Force. You can cast at the Force you learned it at or lower, never higher. The minimum is Force 1. (SR3 p.178) Higher Force is harder to resist and produces more Drain. | Damage Level, for combat and elemental spells. You choose L, M, S or D when you cast. That choice is both the spell’s base damage and its base Drain Level. (SR3 p.191, p.196) | How many Sorcery dice go into this spell, and how many Spell Pool dice. You can’t add more pool dice than Sorcery dice. (SR3 p.180) | More than one spell? You can split Sorcery and Spell Pool dice to cast several spells in one Complex Action, up to your Sorcery rating in spells, with at least 1 Sorcery die each. Each spell then gets +2 to its Drain TN for every extra spell. Two spells means +2 on each Drain Test; three means +4 on each. (SR3 p.181) | Sustaining anything? Choose whether to keep or drop spells you’re already sustaining. Each one you keep costs +2 to all your tests, including this Sorcery Test and its Drain Test. (SR3 p.178) | Area spells: the base radius is your Magic in meters, and it hits everyone valid inside, including you and your friends. Withhold Sorcery dice to change it: every 2 dice withheld shrink it by 1 m, or every 1 die withheld widens it by 1 m. (SR3 p.181) | .

200.title: Step 4: Spell Resistance  (SR3 p.183)
200.content: Two different things can reduce the caster’s successes here. Both can happen against the same spell. The target resists . | Any living target that isn’t willing makes a Spell Resistance Test: its targeted attribute (usually Body, Intelligence or Willpower) against TN = the spell’s Force. | No modifiers apply unless the spell says so. That includes the target’s wounds. (SR3 p.183) | Non-living, non-magical targets don’t resist. | . How The 2nd Chumming reads it: a target who is sustaining spells still takes +2 per spell on this test. The book says both “no target modifiers apply to this test” (SR3 p.183) and that sustaining costs +2 on “all tests, including Drain Resistance Tests (but not normal Damage Resistance Tests)” (SR3 p.178). The maintainer ruled that p.178’s “all tests” wins (2026-09-14). Wounds still don’t apply. A magician blocks it: Spell Defense (SR3 p.183) . | At some earlier point, a magician set aside Sorcery and Spell Pool dice for defense. That’s a Free Action. | They can protect up to their Sorcery rating in subjects, all within Magic × 100 m and on the same plane. Protecting yourself counts as one. | When a protected subject is targeted, the defender senses it and may roll any of those dice against TN = the spell’s Force. It takes no action. | Every success subtracts one success from the caster’s Sorcery Test. If that takes the caster to 0 or less, the spell fails. | Dice used are gone until the next Combat Turn. | .

201.title: Step 5: Spell Effect  (SR3 p.183, p.191)
201.content: Compare the caster’s remaining successes with the target’s resistance successes. | Target ties or wins: no effect. A tie goes to the target. | Caster wins: the net successes (caster − target) measure the effect. The spell’s description says what they buy. | No resistance roll (an object, or a willing subject): all the caster’s successes count, and 1 success always gives some effect. | Damaging spells: the chosen Damage Level stages up one level per 2 net successes, up to Deadly. | . Combat spells: armor doesn’t help (SR3 p.191) . Combat spells (Manabolt, Powerbolt, Stunbolt and their ball versions) damage the target directly and bypass armor. The Spell Resistance Test is the target’s only defense, so there’s no Damage Resistance Test. Mana spells are resisted with Willpower and affect only living and magical targets. Physical spells are resisted with Body and can hit objects too. | Spell | Type | Resisted by | Drain | Damage | . | Stunbolt / Stunball | Mana | Willpower | −1(Damage Level) / −1(Damage Level +1) | Stun | . | Manabolt / Manaball | Mana | Willpower | (Damage Level) / (Damage Level +1) | Physical | . | Powerbolt / Powerball | Physical | Body | +1(Damage Level) / +1(Damage Level +1) | Physical | . | Death Touch | Mana | Willpower | (Damage Level −1) | Physical, by touch | . Elemental spells work like guns (SR3 p.183, p.196) . Fireball, Flamethrower, Lightning Bolt, Acid Stream and similar spells make real fire, lightning or acid. They follow the ranged combat rules, so steps 3 to 5 change: . | Sorcery is the ranged combat skill. The base TN is 4 at any range if you can see the target, plus cover, visibility, injury and sustaining modifiers. Spell Pool dice can be added. (SR3 p.183) | The target can dodge with Combat Pool. (SR3 p.183) | Instead of a Spell Resistance Test, the target makes a Damage Resistance Test with Body plus Combat Pool dice, and Impact armor at half its rating (rounded down) protects. (SR3 p.183, p.196) | The chosen Damage Level stages up 2 successes per level for the caster and down for the target, as in ordinary ranged combat. (SR3 p.183) | Secondary effects can still set fires, cook off ammunition or melt material, even if the primary damage is staged to nothing. (SR3 p.196) | . Glass and walls do block elemental spells, which have to break through like bullets. Targets hidden behind cover inside a Fireball’s radius still get hit. Spell Defense and astral barriers still work against them. (SR3 p.182) . The damage Power of an elemental spell. The core book gives the spell’s Damage Code but never states its Power in so many words. The usual reading is that the Power is the spell’s Force, so a Force 6 Fireball cast at Moderate is 6M before staging.

202.title: Step 6: Drain  (SR3 p.162, p.180, p.183, p.191)
202.content: Right after casting, in the same action, whether or not the spell worked, the caster resists Drain. Reading a Drain code (SR3 p.191) . A spell’s Drain looks like +1(M) or -1(Damage Level +1): . | The number outside the brackets modifies the Power, which is the target number: Drain Power = Force ÷ 2, rounded down, + that modifier. | The part inside the brackets is the Drain Level, the damage you take before resisting. For combat and elemental spells it’s the Damage Level you chose, adjusted by any modifier written with it. | If a modifier would push the Drain Level above Deadly, add +2 Drain Power per level above instead. | . Adding up the TN . | Source | Change | . | Base | Force ÷ 2 (round down) + the spell’s modifier | . | Each spell you’re sustaining | +2 (p.178, p.180) | . | Each extra spell cast in the same action | +2 (p.181) | . | The Sorcery Test came up all 1s | +2 (p.182) | . Otherwise, no modifiers apply, including wounds. (SR3 p.183) . The roll . The caster rolls Willpower plus any number of Spell Pool dice. There’s no cap here, unlike the Sorcery Test. Every 2 successes lower the Drain Level one step. Below Light, you take nothing. (SR3 p.44, p.183) . Stun or Physical? (SR3 p.162, p.183) . | Stun normally. | Physical if the Force is higher than your Magic, or if you’re astrally projecting, whatever the Force. | A limited spell (fetish −1, exclusive −2) can lower the Force for Drain purposes, both for the TN and for this Stun-or-Physical check. (SR3 p.180) | Physical damage from Drain can’t be healed by magic, only by rest and medical care. (SR3 p.162) | .

203.content: | Duration | What it means | . | Instant (I) | Takes effect and ends at once. The results, such as wounds, stay. Combat spells work this way. | . | Sustained (S) | Lasts while you concentrate, which takes no action. | . | Permanent (P) | Must be sustained for a base time, then becomes permanent. Sorcery successes can be spent dividing that time instead of on the effect. | . While sustaining: . | +2 to all your tests per sustained spell, including Drain Resistance but not ordinary Damage Resistance. | You can sustain up to your Sorcery rating in spells at once. | If you take damage, roll Sorcery against the spell’s Force (plus injury modifiers) to keep it going. | Dropping a spell is a Free Action. Being knocked out or falling asleep drops them all. | An Exclusive Action means dropping every sustained spell first. | . A sustaining focus holds a spell for you, and the +2 doesn’t apply to you. (SR3 p.191) .

204.title: Worked example: Manabolt
204.content: Kestrel has Magic 6, Sorcery 5, and a Spell Pool of 4 (Intelligence 5, Willpower 5, Magic 6 → 16 ÷ 3 = 5, and she spent 1 earlier this turn). She casts Manabolt at Force 5, choosing Serious, at a guard with Willpower 4. She isn’t sustaining anything. | Preparation. Force 5, Serious, 5 Sorcery dice plus 3 Spell Pool dice. That leaves 1 pool die for Drain. | Targeting. She can see him and they’re both on the physical plane. | Sorcery Test. 8 dice against TN 4 (his Willpower). She gets 4 successes. | Resistance. The guard rolls Willpower 4 against TN 5 (the Force) and gets 1. Nobody is running Spell Defense for him. | Effect. 4 − 1 = 3 net successes. Two of them stage Serious up to Deadly; the third is left over. Combat spells ignore armor, so the guard takes a Deadly Physical wound. | Drain. Manabolt’s Drain is (Damage Level). Power is 5 ÷ 2 = 2, and the level is Serious, the level she chose, not the staged one. She rolls Willpower 5 plus her last Spell Pool die, 6 dice against TN 2, and gets 3 successes. Two of them take Serious down to Moderate. Force 5 isn’t higher than her Magic 6, so it’s Moderate Stun. | . If she had cast at Force 7 (assuming she’d learned it that high): Drain Power would be 3, and the Drain would be Physical, because 7 is higher than her Magic. If a mage were protecting the guard with Spell Defense and rolled 2 successes against TN 5, Kestrel’s 4 would drop to 2. The guard’s 1 resistance success would leave 1 net success: not enough to stage up, so he’d take Serious.

207.content: Each spell in the Street Grimoire is given as Type · Target · Duration · Drain. Its category is the section it’s listed in. | Statistic | Values | What it means | . | Type | M (mana) or P (physical) | Physical spells affect physical properties, and only they affect non-living objects. Mana spells affect minds, spirits, life force and magic, and only they affect astral forms (SR3 p.178). | . | Target | W, B, I, OR, or a number | The target number. W, B and I are the target’s Willpower, Body and Intelligence; OR is the Object Resistance Table (SR3 p.182). An unwilling target also makes a Spell Resistance Test (SR3 p.191). | . | Duration | I, S or P | Instant, Sustained or Permanent. See Sustaining spells (SR3 p.178). | . | Drain | e.g. +1(M) | A modifier to the Drain Power, which is half the Force rounded down, and the Drain Level (SR3 p.191). | . Range. Most spells are line of sight: if the caster can see the target, at any distance, it can be affected. Some, especially health spells, need a touch. Touching an unwilling target takes an unarmed attack, at −1 TN, as part of the spellcasting; one net success is enough (SR3 p.178). Spells that do or heal damage have a Drain Level that depends on the damage. If a modifier would push the Drain Level past Deadly, each level past Deadly adds +2 to the Drain Power instead (SR3 p.191). Example. A Force 6 Fireball cast at Serious has Drain +1(Damage Level +2). Power: 6 ÷ 2 = 3, + 1 = 4. Level: Serious + 2 is one level past Deadly, so the level is Deadly and the Power rises by 2, to 6. The caster resists 6D Drain. Permanent spells (SR3 p.178) . Worked example. A mage learns Manabolt at Force 5 from a formula. Manabolt’s Drain is the damage level, so the formula is priced at its highest, D: 5 × 1,000¥ = 5,000¥, availability 5 / 7 days. She needs a Sorcery library of rating 5 or more. Her Sorcery Test is against 5 × 2 = TN 10. With 1 success it takes 5 ÷ 1 = 5 days, and it costs 5 Good Karma. Limited spells (SR3 p.180–181) . A limit makes a spell easier, in one of two ways, chosen when you learn it: it either lowers the Force for Drain (including whether the Drain is Physical), or lowers the Karma cost and the learning TN, by its modifier. | Limit | Modifier | The catch | . | Fetish | −1 | The fetish, an enchanted reusable object for one spell category, must be touching you to cast. Losing it means attuning a new one: hours of meditation equal to the Force. | . | Exclusive | −2 | Casting and sustaining it is an Exclusive Action (p.160). | . A spell can have both, if they’re for different purposes. An unlimited version has to be learned separately. The book’s example (SR3 p.181): Grandfather Bones, Magic 6, learns Fireball at Force 8 with the exclusive limit. Taken off Drain, he treats it as Force 6 for Drain, so the Drain isn’t Physical. 211.title: Doing it in The 2nd Chumming (Foundry)
211.content: Getting a spell onto the sheet . Drag a spell onto the character from the compendiums (Shadowrun 3rd, Magic in the Shadows and State of the Art 2064 under Spells), and it appears on the Magic tab with a Cast button. Set its learned Force on the spell. A spell with a Force can be cast at that Force or lower, never higher (SR3 p.178). A spell with no Force recorded isn’t capped, and the cast dialog says so. Learning with Karma . On the Bio tab, Spend Karma… lists each spell on the sheet under Magic. Pick one, enter the Force to learn it at, and any limit modifier taken off the cost. It charges Good Karma equal to the Force, less the limit (SR3 p.180–181), and records the new Force. The purchase goes into the 📒 Ledger, and the GM can undo it there. The Sorcery Test to learn, the days of study, and the teacher’s or formula’s price are the GM’s to run. A limit taken off Drain instead is recorded on the spell, and the cast drains at the lowered Force (SR3 p.180). Casting . Cast opens the Force dialog, then the target, then Spell Pool, and rolls. Every step after that, from resistance to Drain, is on Spellcasting, Resistance & Drain.

219.title: Why the syndicates matter
219.content: The SR3 introduction says the Mafia, the Yakuza and the other syndicates “have grown explosively”, because their networks supply anything people will buy (SR3 p.8). In Seattle, the city’s position as a UCAS island inside NAN territory, near the sea route to Russia, makes it a major smuggling port for every syndicate (NS p.82). The syndicates hire runners through street Johnsons, who have less money than corp Johnsons but can offer protection, illegal services or extra bodies (MJLBB p.18).

240.title: Doing it in The 2nd Chumming (Foundry)
240.content: Getting a weapon . Drag a weapon onto the character from the compendiums, or buy it with 🛒 Buy gear. It appears on the Weapons tab. Its category picks the skill and the range bands; Range override on the weapon replaces the bands, as “5/15/30/50”. Shooting . | ✋ marks a weapon ready in hand; drawing one is a Ready Weapon action (SR3 p.107). | The 🎲 on the row opens the attack. Choose the fire mode and, for full-auto, the rounds. The dialog shows the range band measured on the map, the recoil after compensation (the weapon’s own and the character’s, both editable), the target count for this phase, and every other modifier. The TN is yours to change before you roll. | Smartgun, laser sight and recoil compensation are fields on the weapon. A smartgun saves the rounds walked fire would waste. | A shotgun loaded with shot asks for the choke, and the card shows each spread’s Power and TN. | 🎯 on the token’s HUD fires a ready weapon from the map. | . Ammunition . | ↻ Reload loads from ammunition on the character: loose rounds of the gun’s class, or a spare clip. The loaded type (regular, APDS, explosive, gel, flechette, tracer, shot) changes the damage and the armor used on the soak card by itself. | With the world setting Track ammunition on, firing counts rounds down, and an empty gun won’t fire until reloaded. | Thrown weapons count down their quantity; bows and crossbows nock an arrow or bolt. | . Melee . Equip a melee weapon on the Weapons tab, then use its 🎲 Melee attack. Reach is read from the weapon. Unarmed is always there, and uses the best of Unarmed Combat and any martial art. See Actions & Combat.
